title: A plant's life cycle: how a seed grows into a plant that makes new seeds
playtest: Every experiment, activity, game, challenge and project was walked through as if done at home. Changes made: Flower to Fruit now says which plants work and how fast (bhindi pods in 5 or 6 days, tomatoes much slower), to tag flowers on the morning they open, and that some flowers will drop. That is a real result, not a failure. A nursery chilli or brinjal is the fallback. Inside the Fruit counts small fruits fully and big ones by counting one part and multiplying, so it fits in 25 minutes. It says the banana's specks are not real seeds. Be Edmond needs a pumpkin, gourd or cucumber vine, so it is not in the core or spine. It now says to bag the buds the evening before, to do it before 10 in the morning (lauki and tori in the evening), and that young vines make only male flowers at first. Floating Leaves gives exact amounts, how many syringe pulls are needed, a fix if the circles will not sink, and how long they take to float in sun or lamplight. Kitchen to Kitchen says when to sow moong (warm months), the 5 hours of sun they need, the winter switch to matar, common pests, and to pick pods when black before they pop. The onion test warns that some shop onions do not sprout, and that the onion rots if sat too deep. Both games say how to play alone, and Time Detective has a hidden-card puzzle for one player. Parents should know: Kitchen to Kitchen takes about 75 days and needs a sunny spot. Be Edmond and Adopt a Tree depend on having a vine or tree nearby.

summary.text: Every fruit in your kitchen was once a flower, and every seed inside it can grow into a new plant. A life cycle is all the stages of a living thing's life, until they make young of their own. A flowering plant goes from seed to seedling to grown plant. Then they flower, each flower can grow into a fruit, and the fruit holds new seeds. Your child opens kitchen fruits to find the seeds and the flower's leftovers, and can grow moong from seed to seed in two to three months. Then the unit follows the idea further: plants built mostly from air and water, plants that measure the length of the night, and bamboo that flowers only once, after about 48 years.
summary.art: A big circle drawn like a clock face: a moong seed at the top, then a seedling, a leafy plant, a yellow flower, a green pod and black pods spilling new seeds back to the top.

intro.hook: Look at a tomato, or a brinjal. See the little green star, or the green cap, at the top? Where do you think it came from? Here is a clue. Not long ago, this whole tomato was a small yellow flower.
intro.text: Every fruit in your kitchen was once a flower. Every seed inside it can grow into a plant that makes flowers again. Put a moong seed in a pot today. In two to three months, if they get sun and water, they will give you back a whole handful of moong. Which part of a flower turns into the fruit? And why does the plant end up exactly where they started, as seeds?
intro.art: A child holding a tomato up close, the green star of sepals on top glowing, with a faint drawing behind it of the yellow tomato flower it came from.

outcomes: I can name the stages of a flowering plant's life cycle in order: seed, seedling, grown plant, flower, fruit and new seeds.
I can explain that a fruit grows from a flower and holds the seeds. I can find the flower's leftover parts on a fruit.
I can explain why it is called a cycle: the new seeds grow into new plants, so the stages start again.
I can watch a real plant change over days and weeks. I can measure it and record it in a table, a bar chart or a line graph.
I can give examples of plants with short and long life cycles, and of plants that grow new plants without seeds.
I can explain that a plant builds their body mostly from air and water, using sunlight, and gives it back when they die.
I can say what scientists agree on about plant life cycles, and what they still do not know, such as how bamboo counts the years.

terms.meaning: All the stages a living thing goes through, from the start of their life until they make young ones of their own. Then the stages start again.
terms.example: Moong: seed, seedling, grown plant, flower, pod, new seeds.
terms.art: A circle of arrows joining a seed, a seedling, a plant, a flower, a pod and seeds.

terms.meaning: One step or part of a life cycle.
terms.example: Being a seedling is one stage. Flowering is another stage.
terms.art: A row of stepping stones, each with a picture of one stage of a plant's life.

terms.meaning: A baby plant packed in a coat, with their own store of food.
terms.example: A moong seed, a rajma bean and the big seed inside a mango stone are all seeds.
terms.art: A moong seed, a mango stone and a rajma bean side by side.

terms.meaning: A very young plant that has just come out of their seed. They have a tiny root, a short stem and their first leaves.
terms.example: The small green shoots in a tray of sprouted methi are seedlings.
terms.art: A tray of tiny methi seedlings with two leaves each.

terms.meaning: The first leaves, which were already folded up inside the seed. They are often thick and round, and hold food.
terms.example: The two round leaves at the top of a new bean plant.
terms.art: A young bean plant with two fat round seed leaves and two pointed true leaves above them.

terms.meaning: The leaves that grow after the seed leaves. They have the plant's own leaf shape, and they make food from sunlight.
terms.example: A tomato seedling's true leaves are jagged and smell of tomato.
terms.art: A tomato seedling with round seed leaves at the bottom and jagged true leaves above.

terms.meaning: A plant that is big enough and old enough to make flowers. Scientists call this a mature plant.
terms.example: A moong plant starts to flower when they are about one month old.
terms.art: A bushy moong plant in a pot with their first small yellow flowers.

terms.meaning: A flower, or a leaf, before it opens. It is folded up tight.
terms.example: A rose bud, or the tight green tip at the end of a stem.
terms.art: A tight hibiscus bud next to the same flower fully open.

terms.meaning: The part of a plant that makes seeds. Many flowers are bright and sweet-smelling. That brings insects and birds to visit them.
terms.example: A hibiscus, a marigold, and the small yellow flowers on a moong plant.
terms.art: A hibiscus flower with a bee flying towards it.

terms.meaning: The soft, often coloured parts around the middle of a flower.
terms.example: A marigold has many orange petals. A hibiscus has five.
terms.art: A hibiscus with its five red petals labelled.

terms.meaning: The small green leaf-like parts that wrap a flower bud before it opens. On many fruits they stay on, like a green star or a cap.
terms.example: The green cap on a brinjal and the green star on a tomato are sepals.
terms.art: A brinjal with its green cap and a tomato with its green star, both glowing.

terms.meaning: A fine dust made by flowers, usually yellow. It must reach the middle of a flower before the flower can make seeds.
terms.example: The yellow dust left on your finger after touching the middle of a hibiscus.
terms.art: A magnified speck of yellow pollen on the tip of a flower's stalk.

terms.meaning: Pollen being carried to the sticky tip in the middle of a flower. Wind, insects, birds, bats or people can carry it. Only then can most flowers grow a fruit with seeds.
terms.example: A bee covered in yellow dust flying from one pumpkin flower to another.
terms.art: A bee dusted with pollen landing in the middle of a pumpkin flower.

terms.meaning: The part of a plant that grows from a flower and holds the seeds. To a scientist, a tomato, a bhindi and a chilli are all fruits.
terms.example: A mango, a pea pod, a cucumber and a bhindi are all fruits.
terms.art: A mango, a pea pod, a cucumber and a bhindi cut open to show their seeds.

terms.meaning: A long fruit that holds a row of seeds. It often splits open when it is ripe.
terms.example: Pea pods, moong pods and drumsticks.
terms.art: An open pea pod with a row of green peas.

terms.meaning: Fully grown and ready. A ripe fruit often changes colour and gets soft or sweet. Its seeds are ready to grow.
terms.example: A green mango turns yellow and sweet when it is ripe.
terms.art: A green mango beside a ripe yellow mango.

terms.meaning: A plant that goes through their whole life cycle in one year or less, then dies.
terms.example: Moong, rice, wheat and marigold are annuals.
terms.art: A dry, brown moong plant with black pods, their life cycle finished.

terms.meaning: A plant that lives for many years and can flower again and again.
terms.example: Mango, neem, coconut, rose and tulsi are perennials.
terms.art: A big old mango tree in flower.

terms.meaning: A piece of a plant, like a stem or a leaf, that can grow roots and become a new plant without a seed.
terms.example: A money plant stem in a bottle of water grows roots.
terms.art: A money plant stem in a glass bottle with white roots growing.

terms.meaning: A living thing that is an exact copy of their parent. Plants grown from cuttings are clones.
terms.example: All the banana plants of one kind on a farm are copies, grown from shoots of the same parent plants.
terms.art: A row of identical banana plants, joined by a dotted line to one parent plant.

terms.meaning: How green leaves make food. They take in carbon dioxide from the air and water from the roots. They use the energy of sunlight to turn these into sugar, and they give out oxygen.
terms.example: A tulsi plant in the sun is making sugar right now.
terms.art: A leaf in sunshine with arrows: air and water going in, sugar and oxygen coming out.

terms.meaning: A gas in the air, which you breathe out. Plants take it in and build their bodies from it.
terms.example: Every breath you breathe out has carbon dioxide in it.
terms.art: A child breathing out near a plant, with little arrows of air going into their leaves.

terms.meaning: A living thing that breaks down dead plants and animals. It puts their minerals back into the soil and their carbon back into the air.
terms.example: Mushrooms, earthworms and tiny bacteria in a compost pit.
terms.art: A fallen leaf being broken down by an earthworm, mushrooms and tiny dots of bacteria.

explanations.definition: A life cycle is all the stages a living thing goes through, from the start of their life until they make young ones. For a flowering plant the stages are: seed, seedling, grown plant, flower, fruit, and new seeds.
explanations.description: It is called a cycle because it goes round in a circle. The last stage, new seeds, is also the first stage of the next plant. So the circle never really ends. A moong seed grows into a moong plant. The plant makes flowers. The flowers turn into pods. The pods hold new moong seeds, and each one can start again. You can start drawing the circle at any stage. A seed is not more of a 'beginning' than a flower is.
examples: Moong: seed, seedling, grown plant, yellow flower, green pod, black pod full of new seeds.
Mango: mango stone, seedling, young tree, mango flowers, mangoes, new mango stones.
Marigold: seed, seedling, plant, orange flower, dry flower head full of thin black seeds.
explanations.art: A circle of six pictures joined by arrows: a moong seed, a seedling, a bushy plant, a yellow flower, a green pod, and a black pod with seeds.
explanations.context: This card explains the main idea of the whole unit: what a plant's life cycle is, and why it is a circle.

explanations.definition: A seed wakes up when they get water, warmth and air. This is called germination. Their root comes out first and grows down. Then their shoot grows up into the light, and the plant becomes a seedling.
explanations.description: The unit 'Seeds and how they sprout' tells this part of the story in detail. Here is the short version. At first, the seedling lives on the food packed inside the seed. Many seedlings first show two round seed leaves, which were folded up inside the seed. Soon the true leaves grow above them. True leaves have the plant's own leaf shape. Once they open, the seedling can make their own food from sunlight. The seed leaves are no longer needed. They shrink, go yellow and fall off.
examples: A bean seedling has two fat seed leaves first, then pointed true leaves.
A rice or maize seedling comes up as one thin green spike.
explanations.art: Three steps: a bean splitting with a root going down, a hooked shoot coming up, and a seedling with two round seed leaves and two true leaves.
explanations.context: A life cycle starts again every time a seed sprouts. This card is a short reminder of how a seed becomes a seedling.

explanations.concept: Growing up: leaves make food from sunlight
explanations.definition: A growing plant makes their own food in their green leaves. This is called photosynthesis. Leaves take in carbon dioxide from the air and water from the roots. Using the energy of sunlight, they turn them into sugar. They give out oxygen.
explanations.description: The plant uses the sugar in two ways. They use some for energy, the way your body uses food. They also use sugar to build new stems, leaves and roots. So a plant grows mainly by making more of themselves out of air and water. A plant grows slowly at first, then fast, then slowly again once they are grown. The chart shows a made-up example for a moong plant in a pot. They grow fastest in weeks 3 to 5. After about week 6 they put their effort into flowers and pods instead of getting taller.
examples: A plant kept in a dark cupboard grows pale, thin and floppy, then dies. They cannot make food.
Leaves turn to face the window. They are reaching for light.
explanations.art: A moong plant in a pot in sunlight, with arrows showing air going into the leaves, water coming up from the roots and tiny bubbles of oxygen coming out.
explanations.context: Between the seedling stage and the flower stage, a plant must grow big. This card explains how they make the food to do that.

chart.title: Made-up example: height of a moong plant in a pot, week by week
chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show the usual shape: slow, then fast, then slow. Your plant will be different.

explanations.concept: When a plant is ready to flower
explanations.definition: A plant flowers when they are big enough, and when the season is right. Many plants find out the season by measuring how long the nights are.
explanations.description: A young plant first grows leaves and roots. When they have grown enough, the tips of some stems stop making leaves and make flower buds instead. Many plants wait for the right season too. In 1920, two American scientists, Wightman Garner and Harry Allard, found that some tobacco and soybean plants flower only when the days get short. In 1938, Karl Hamner and James Bonner showed that what the plant really measures is the length of the night. Flash a light in the middle of a long night, and those plants do not flower. The leaves do the measuring. Then they send a message up the stem to the buds. A Russian scientist, Mikhail Chailakhyan, guessed in 1936 that such a message must exist. It took until 2007 for scientists to find it. It is a protein that travels from the leaves to the bud.
examples: Rice in many parts of India flowers when the nights get longer after the monsoon.
Some plants, like wheat in cold countries, wait until they have felt a cold winter.
Many kinds of moong flower about 30 to 40 days after sowing in warm weather, whatever the day length.
explanations.art: A plant under a moon and stars with a long night shown on a clock, and a glowing message travelling from a leaf up the stem to a flower bud.
explanations.context: How does a plant know when it is time to stop growing leaves and start making flowers? This card explains.

explanations.concept: A flower is where the fruit will grow
explanations.definition: A flower is the part of a plant that makes seeds. In its middle is a swollen base with tiny seed-starts inside. When pollen reaches the sticky tip above that base, the base can grow into a fruit, and the seed-starts can grow into seeds.
explanations.description: Look at a flower from the outside in. First come the green sepals, which wrapped the bud. Then come the petals, often bright and scented, which bring in visitors. Next come thin stalks with yellow dust on their tips. The stalks are called stamens, and the dust is pollen. In the very middle is a part shaped a little like a bottle. Its base is the ovary. Scientists call the tiny seed-starts inside it ovules. Pollen must be carried to the sticky tip of the bottle, which is called the stigma. This is called pollination. Insects, birds, bats, wind or people can carry it. Some flowers, like moong, peas and tomato, can pollinate themselves. After that, the petals fall off and the base starts to swell. That swelling base is the baby fruit. You will learn much more about pollination in the Class 4 unit on flowers.
examples: In a pumpkin flower, you can see the baby pumpkin as a little green ball behind the petals.
A bhindi flower opens for just one morning. Five days later, a finger-long pod is in its place.
explanations.art: A flower cut in half and labelled from outside in: sepals, petals, pollen stalks, and the bottle-shaped middle with its swollen base full of tiny seed-starts.
explanations.context: Every fruit you eat was once a flower. This card shows which part of the flower becomes the fruit.

explanations.concept: A fruit is a flower's base grown big, holding seeds
explanations.definition: To a scientist, a fruit is the part that grows from a flower's base and holds the seeds. So tomatoes, bhindi, brinjal, cucumber, chillies and pea pods are all fruits.
explanations.description: In the kitchen, we call sweet ones fruits and the others vegetables. Botanists, the scientists who study plants, use a different rule. If it grew from a flower and holds seeds, it is a fruit. You can often see what is left of the flower on a fruit. The green star on top of a tomato and the green cap on a brinjal are the old sepals. The little crown at the end of a pomegranate or a guava is the flower's leftovers too. Each seed inside came from one tiny seed-start in the flower. Some fruits have one seed, like a mango. Others have hundreds, like a papaya.
examples: A pea pod is a fruit. The peas are its seeds.
A pomegranate's crown is the remains of its red flower.
A banana's dark tip is where its flower was.
explanations.art: Kitchen fruits cut open in a row, each with an arrow to its flower leftovers: tomato star, brinjal cap, pomegranate crown, banana tip.
explanations.context: Is a tomato a fruit or a vegetable? This card explains what a fruit is to a scientist, and how to spot the flower's leftovers on it.

explanations.concept: Why plants make fruits: sending seeds away
explanations.definition: A fruit protects the seeds and helps them travel away from the parent plant. Many fruits are sweet so that animals eat them and drop the seeds somewhere else.
explanations.description: A seed that falls right under their parent has to compete with them for light and water. A seed carried far away has a better chance. So plants have many ways of sending their seeds away. Sweet fruits are eaten by birds, bats, monkeys and people. The seeds pass through, or get spat out, far away. Pods can burst and fling their seeds. Some fruits have wings or fluff and fly on the wind. Coconuts float across the sea. Chillies use their hot taste to choose which animals carry their seeds. In 2001, two American scientists, Joshua Tewksbury and Gary Nabhan, found that the hot taste of chillies keeps away mice and other mammals. Mammals chew seeds up. Birds swallow seeds whole and drop them far away. The hot taste does not burn birds at all. You will learn more about how seeds travel in Class 4.
examples: A koel eats a ripe banyan fig and drops the seeds on a far-off wall.
Moong and pea pods dry, twist and pop, flinging their seeds out.
Grass seeds stick to socks and shoes, and get carried home after a walk.
explanations.art: A bulbul eating a red chilli, a mouse turning away from the chilli, and seeds dropping from the bird far away.
explanations.context: Why does a plant wrap their seeds in sweet fruit? This card explains how fruits help seeds travel.

explanations.definition: Some plants finish their whole life cycle in a few weeks or months, then die. They are called annuals. Others live for many years and flower again and again. They are called perennials.
explanations.description: Moong goes from seed to seed in two to three months. Rice takes about four months. A mango tree grown from a stone usually takes five to eight years before their first mangoes, and then they fruit every year for a long time. Some plants wait for years, flower just once, and then die. The neelakurinji shrub, which grows in the hills of Kerala and Tamil Nadu, flowers all together only once every 12 years. Their last big bloom near Munnar was in 2018. One kind of bamboo in Mizoram waits about 48 years. Then all the plants of that kind flower together, make their seeds, and die. The talipot palm can wait more than 30 years. Then they make one of the biggest bunches of flowers of any plant, and die.
examples: Short: moong, methi, marigold and mustard, from seed to seed in a few months.
Long: mango, neem and coconut, which flower for years and years.
Once in a long life: neelakurinji every 12 years, and bamboo after about 48 years.
explanations.art: A row of plants under a long timeline: a moong plant at 2 to 3 months, rice at 4 months, a mango tree at 6 years, neelakurinji hills turning blue at 12 years, a bamboo grove flowering at 48 years.
explanations.context: Some plants live for a few weeks and some for hundreds of years. This card compares how long different plants take to go round their life cycle.

chart.title: About how long from sowing a seed to the plant's first new seeds
rows: Thale cress, a tiny plant scientists study
Fruits every year for many years
Dies after flowering, new plants grow from their seeds
One kind of bamboo in Mizoram

explanations.definition: Many plants can also grow new plants from a piece of themselves, such as a stem, a leaf, a root or a bulb. The new plant is an exact copy of their parent, called a clone.
explanations.description: A potato is a swollen underground stem. Each 'eye' on it can sprout a new potato plant. An onion is a bulb, made of thick leaves wrapped round a short stem. Put its bottom in water and it grows new roots and green leaves. A money plant stem grows roots in a bottle of water. Sugarcane is planted as pieces of stem. A leaf of the patharchatta plant, also called Bryophyllum, laid on damp soil grows tiny new plants from the notches along its edges. The bananas we eat have no proper seeds. Farmers grow new banana plants from shoots at the base of the old one. Copies are quick and easy. But they are risky. In the 1950s, a disease wiped out most of the world's favourite banana, the Gros Michel, because every plant was a copy with the same weakness. A new form of that disease now threatens today's banana, the Cavendish.
examples: An old potato in a dark basket grows white shoots from its eyes.
A rose cutting pushed into damp soil can grow into a new rose bush.
Grass spreads by stems that creep along the ground.
explanations.art: A potato with shoots from its eyes, an onion in a glass growing roots, and a patharchatta leaf with tiny plants along its edge.
explanations.context: Not every new plant grows from a seed. This card is about plants that make copies of themselves from a piece.

explanations.concept: Deep down: a plant is built from air
explanations.definition: Most of a plant's body is made from carbon dioxide taken from the air, and water. Only a very small part comes from the soil.
explanations.description: This surprises almost everyone, including grown-ups. In the 1600s, a Flemish scientist, Jan Baptist van Helmont, tried a test. He put a small willow tree in a big pot of dried, weighed soil. For five years he gave the tree only rainwater. The tree grew from about 2 kilograms to about 77 kilograms. The soil lost only about 60 grams. He thought the tree was made of water. He was partly right. We now know most of their dry wood is made of carbon atoms taken from carbon dioxide in the air. In the 1950s, Melvin Calvin and his team in California followed carbon atoms from the air into the sugar a plant made. They used a special kind of carbon they could track. A big neem tree is mostly air and water, put together with the energy of sunlight. The soil gives the plant small amounts of important things, called minerals, like iron and nitrogen.
examples: When wood burns, it turns back into carbon dioxide and water vapour, and only a little ash is left. The ash is the part that came from the soil.
A pot plant can grow for years without the pot getting much emptier of soil.
explanations.art: A huge neem tree with a cut-away showing the tree built of tiny atoms drifting in from the air, and only a thin trickle coming up from the soil.
explanations.context: Where does a big tree's body come from? This card answers, and the answer surprises most grown-ups.

explanations.definition: When a plant dies, decomposers break them down. Their atoms go back into the soil and the air, and new plants are built from them.
explanations.description: Fungi like mushrooms, tiny bacteria, earthworms, termites and woodlice all feed on dead leaves and stems. As they eat, they break the plant into smaller and smaller pieces. Some of their carbon goes back into the air as carbon dioxide. Their minerals go back into the soil. The next seeds use that air and soil to grow. So the same atoms go round and round through plants, animals, soil and air. The life cycle of a plant sits inside a much bigger cycle of atoms. The carbon in your body was once in plants too, because all your food comes from plants, or from animals that ate plants.
examples: A pile of fallen leaves under a tree is gone by the next year. Decomposers ate it.
A compost pit turns kitchen peels into dark, crumbly soil in a few months.
explanations.art: A dead plant lying on soil, with mushrooms, earthworms and bacteria breaking them down, and arrows showing atoms going into the air and soil and up into a new seedling.
explanations.context: A plant's life cycle ends when they die, or does it? This card follows what happens to a plant's body after death.

explanations.concept: Every seed carries a copy of the plant's instructions
explanations.definition: Every cell of a plant holds a long set of instructions for building that plant. The instructions are written in a chemical called DNA. Each seed gets a copy from their parents.
explanations.description: That is why a moong seed always grows into moong, never into mango. The instructions are copied again and again, from plant to seed to plant, all the way round the life cycle. When pollen from one plant reaches the flower of another, the seed gets some instructions from each parent. So seeds are a little different from each other, just as brothers and sisters are. Between 1856 and 1863, a monk called Gregor Mendel grew thousands of pea plants in his monastery garden in Brno, now in the Czech Republic. He chose peas because they go round their life cycle in one season. He found patterns in how things like seed colour were passed on. When he published his work in 1866, almost nobody noticed. It was rediscovered in 1900, after he had died. Today he is called the father of genetics, the science of how living things pass on their features.
examples: Mango seeds from one sweet tree can grow into trees with quite different mangoes. So farmers join a twig of their best tree onto a young tree. This is called grafting, and the twig grows mangoes just like its parent's.
Every rice plant in a field grew from instructions copied from earlier rice plants, going back thousands of years.
explanations.art: A pea pod open with peas, each pea holding a tiny glowing scroll of instructions, and Mendel's garden behind it.
explanations.context: Why does a moong seed always grow into moong? This card is about the instructions every seed carries.

explanations.concept: Why did flowering plants take over the world?
explanations.description: The first land plants, rather like mosses, appeared over 450 million years ago. Ferns and conifers came long before flowers. The first flowering plants appear in rocks from about 130 million years ago, in the time of the dinosaurs. Then they spread very fast. Today, almost 9 out of every 10 kinds of land plant have flowers. In 1879, Charles Darwin wrote to his friend Joseph Hooker that this sudden spread was 'an abominable mystery'. Scientists still argue about it.
examples: Ferns and mosses have no flowers. They spread by spores, a fine dust, instead of seeds.
Pine trees make seeds in cones, not in flowers or fruits.

perspectives.who: Many scientists who study insects and flowers
perspectives.explanation: Flowers changed together with the insects, birds and bats that visit them. Pollen carried from one plant to another made new kinds of plant appear faster.

perspectives.who: Scientists who study how plants grow
perspectives.explanation: Flowering plants grow fast and finish their life cycles quickly, so they could take over open land before slower plants.
Fruits let animals carry seeds far and wide. Some also point to changes in the climate and the land at the time. Most think several of these worked together.

explanations.art: A dinosaur-age landscape of ferns and conifers, with the first small flowers appearing at the edge and a few early insects visiting them.
explanations.context: Flowers have not always existed. This card is about a puzzle Charles Darwin called 'an abominable mystery'.

explanations.concept: How does bamboo count the years?
explanations.description: Melocanna bamboo in Mizoram flowers about every 48 years. All the clumps across hundreds of kilometres flower together, even clumps planted far apart. Then they make huge numbers of fruits and die. In 1958 and again from 2006 to 2008, the flowering fed so many rats that they multiplied and then ate the farmers' crops. People there call this mautam, and it caused famine. How the bamboo keeps time for so long, and stays in step, is not known. Nobody has found a 48-year clock inside a plant.
examples: Neelakurinji in the Nilgiri and Munnar hills flowers together every 12 years.
Bamboo of one kind planted in another country can still flower at about the same time as their family back home.

perspectives.who: Daniel Janzen, an American scientist, in 1976
perspectives.explanation: Flowering all together makes more seeds than the rats and birds can eat, so some survive. Plants that flowered out of step had their few seeds eaten, so the habit spread.
The plants may count something inside them, like rounds of growth, rather than years. Or the weather may nudge them. Nobody has proved how it works.

explanations.art: A green hillside of bamboo all flowering at once, with a giant question-mark clock in the sky.
explanations.context: Some plants wait many years and then flower all at once. This card is about an open puzzle: how do they keep count?

explanations.definition: Plants can go through their whole life cycle in space. In 1982, small thale cress plants grown on the Soviet space station Salyut 7 flowered and made seeds. They were the first plants known to go from seed to seed in space.
explanations.description: In space, there is no 'down' to guide the roots, so astronauts and scientists must help plants grow. Since then, wheat, peas, lettuce, zinnia flowers and others have been grown on space stations. Space agencies study this because people living on the Moon or Mars one day will need plants that can keep going round their life cycle there. They will need them for food, and to turn the carbon dioxide that astronauts breathe out back into oxygen.
examples: In 2016, an astronaut on the International Space Station grew orange zinnia flowers.
Astronauts on the International Space Station have eaten lettuce they grew there.
explanations.art: Small white-flowered thale cress plants growing in a box inside a space station, with Earth in the window.
explanations.context: Could a plant grow from seed to seed far from Earth? This card is about plants that did.

agreed.text: Flowering plants go through a life cycle: seed, seedling, grown plant, flower, fruit and new seeds.
agreed.evidence: You can watch it in a pot of moong in two to three months. Farmers have watched it in every field for thousands of years.

agreed.text: A fruit grows from the base of a flower, and holds the seeds.
agreed.evidence: Tag a flower with a thread and watch it every day. The petals fall and the base swells into the fruit. The flower's leftovers often stay on the fruit.

agreed.text: Most flowers make fruit only after pollen reaches the middle of the flower.
agreed.evidence: Cover a pumpkin flower with a paper bag so no insect can reach it, and it shrivels. Add pollen by hand, and it grows. Gardeners and vanilla farmers do this every day.

agreed.text: A plant builds their body mostly from carbon dioxide and water, using sunlight.
agreed.evidence: Van Helmont's willow grew about 75 kilograms while the soil lost about 60 grams. In the 1950s, Melvin Calvin's team followed carbon from the air into a plant's sugar.

agreed.text: Many plants decide when to flower by measuring the length of the night.
agreed.evidence: Experiments since 1920 show that flashing a light in the middle of the night can stop some plants from flowering, or make others flower.

challenging.claim: A plant gets their food and their body from the soil.
challenging.who: A very common idea. Many people still think it today.
challenging.for: Roots grow in the soil, and plants die if the soil dries out. Plants in good soil grow better.
challenging.against: Van Helmont's willow grew about 75 kilograms in five years, but the soil lost only about 60 grams. The soil gives water and small amounts of minerals. The rest of the plant is made from carbon dioxide from the air, using sunlight.
challenging.context: This card is about where a plant's body comes from, and an idea most people believe.

challenging.claim: Tomatoes, bhindi and cucumbers are vegetables, not fruits.
challenging.who: Cooks, shopkeepers, and in 1893 the highest court in the United States
challenging.for: In the kitchen, we use them in curries and salads, not in sweets. In 1893, the US Supreme Court decided that a tomato counts as a vegetable for paying taxes.
challenging.against: To a botanist, anything that grows from a flower and holds seeds is a fruit. Both are useful ways of sorting. They just answer different questions.
challenging.context: This card is about a famous argument: is a tomato a fruit or a vegetable?

challenging.claim: Every plant grows from a seed.
challenging.for: Most plants we grow in gardens and fields do come from seeds.
challenging.against: Potatoes, sugarcane, bananas, money plants and many roses are grown from pieces of the plant instead. Ferns and mosses have no seeds at all. They spread by spores.
challenging.context: This card asks whether all plants really start as seeds.

challenging.claim: When a plant dies, they are wasted.
challenging.for: A dead plant gives no more flowers or fruit, and they look like rubbish.
challenging.against: Decomposers break them down, and their atoms go back to the soil and the air. New plants are built from them. Forests depend on this. A fallen tree feeds thousands of living things for years.
challenging.context: This card is about what a plant's death means for other living things.

challenging.claim: Flowers exist to be beautiful for us.
challenging.who: A common idea, and many poems
challenging.for: People love flowers. We have bred roses and marigolds to be even brighter and bigger.
challenging.against: Flowers existed for about 130 million years before there were people. Their colours, scents and sweet nectar bring insects, birds and bats to carry pollen. Some flowers are dull green and are pollinated by the wind. Our love of them is a happy extra.
challenging.context: Why are flowers bright and sweet-smelling? This card is about an idea many of us have without noticing.

challenging.claim: Edmond Albius, a 12-year-old boy, found the way to make vanilla flowers turn into fruit, in 1841.
challenging.who: Historians of vanilla, and the people of Réunion island
challenging.for: His owner, Ferréol Bellier-Beaumont, wrote letters saying Edmond had found it. Farmers still use his method of a thin stick and a thumb.
challenging.against: A French botanist, Jean Michel Claude Richard, later claimed that he had taught Edmond. And a Belgian botanist, Charles Morren, had made vanilla flowers fruit in a greenhouse a few years earlier, in the 1830s. But Morren's way was slow and was not used on farms.
challenging.context: Vanilla pods are the fruits of an orchid flower. This card is about who gets the credit for making vanilla flowers turn into fruit outside Mexico.

big_questions.q: A life cycle is a circle. So where does it begin: with the seed, or with the flower that made the seed?
big_questions.hint: Try starting your drawing at a different stage each time. Does it change the story?

big_questions.q: A big tree can weigh as much as a truck, but the soil under them hardly gets less. Where did the tree come from?
big_questions.hint: Breathe out onto your hand. What is in your breath that a leaf might want?

big_questions.q: How does a plant know it is the right season to flower, when they have no eyes and no calendar?
big_questions.hint: Think about what changes from summer to winter. Nights get longer or shorter.

big_questions.q: Why do plants put so much food into fruits, and then let animals eat them?
big_questions.hint: What happens to a mango stone after a monkey eats the mango?

big_questions.q: A moong plant dies after their pods ripen. Has their life ended, or have they carried on in their seeds?
big_questions.hint: Is a seed the same plant, or a new one? Could it be both?

big_questions.q: You were once tiny, then a baby, then the size you are now. Are you the same person you were at one year old?
big_questions.hint: What has stayed the same? What has changed completely?

big_questions.q: Edmond Albius was 12 and enslaved when he found how to make vanilla flowers fruit. Why might a grown-up botanist have tried to take the credit?
big_questions.hint: Who wrote the books, and who did the work with their hands, in 1841?

big_questions.q: Bamboo in Mizoram waits about 48 years, flowers once, then dies. What could they gain by waiting so long and flowering all together?
big_questions.hint: Rats and birds eat bamboo seeds. Can they eat them all if every clump makes seeds in the same year?

big_questions.q: The bananas we eat are copies of one plant. Why might it be dangerous for the whole world to grow the same plant?
big_questions.hint: What happens if one disease can harm a plant, and every plant is the same?

big_questions.q: Your food comes from plants, and plants are built mostly from air. So is some of you made of air?
big_questions.hint: Follow a carbon atom from the air into a rice grain, into an idli, and into you.

big_questions.q: If people one day live on Mars, what would a plant need to go round their whole life cycle there?
big_questions.hint: Think of every stage: seed, seedling, flower, fruit. What does each one need?

story.title: Edmond's Thumb
story.note: Edmond, Ferréol Bellier-Beaumont, the vanilla vine and the year 1841 are real. So are Edmond's method, the fight over the credit, his freedom in 1848 and the name Albius. Bellier-Beaumont is said to have shown Edmond how to pollinate watermelon flowers by hand. We changed it to pumpkins. The conversations and the small details are imagined.
text: In 1841, on an island in the Indian Ocean called Bourbon, there grew a vine that would not make fruit. The vine climbed the trees in the garden of a man named Ferréol Bellier-Beaumont. Their leaves were thick and shiny. Every year they covered themselves in pale green flowers that smelled faintly of honey. And every year, by the next evening, each flower had dropped to the ground, and nothing was left behind.

The vine was vanilla. They had come across the sea from Mexico. There, their long pods were dried to make one of the most wonderful smells in the world. In Mexico, the vines hung heavy with pods. But here, and in the hothouses of France, and in the gardens of Java, the vines grew and grew and flowered and flowered, and gave nothing at all. Some people said the plant was homesick.

Edmond was twelve. He was enslaved, which means that Bellier-Beaumont owned him, the way a man might own a cart. The law allowed it then. It was deeply wrong. Edmond's mother had died when he was born, and the old man had brought him up among the plants. Edmond carried water, pulled weeds and followed Bellier-Beaumont along the garden paths. He was always listening.

One morning the old man stopped by the pumpkin patch. 'Look here,' he said. He pointed at two yellow flowers that looked exactly alike. Then he lifted one and turned it over. Behind its petals, where the flower met its stalk, sat a tiny green ball, no bigger than a marble.

'A baby pumpkin,' said Bellier-Beaumont. 'This is a mother flower. That one is a father flower. It has no baby behind it. It only has dust.' He picked the father flower, peeled back its petals, and showed Edmond the yellow powder on the little stalk in its middle. Then he dabbed the powder into the centre of the mother flower, like pressing a stamp onto a letter. 'Now we wait,' he said.

Edmond waited. Two days later, he ran to the pumpkin patch before breakfast. The mother flower's petals had shrivelled. But the green ball behind them had grown to the size of a lime. Another mother flower nearby, which nobody had touched, had gone yellow and soft. When Edmond poked it, it fell off in his hand.

He crouched there for a long time, looking from one to the other. So that was it. A flower was not the end of anything. A flower was a fruit that had not happened yet. Something had to happen first, deep in its middle. The dust had to get in.

That afternoon he went to look at the vanilla vine. Their flowers had already closed. They opened only in the early morning, for a few hours, and never again. So the next day he came back at dawn, when the grass was still wet.

He looked into one flower. He could see no dust anywhere. He looked into a second, and a third. In the middle of each was a little pale column, smooth as candle wax. He touched it gently with a fingertip. At its tip, half-hidden under a tiny cap, was a smear of sticky yellow. The dust! Just below it was a shiny, sticky place, the place where the dust needed to go. But between the two lay a thin flap, like a small tongue, keeping them apart.
Today, people think that in Mexico, certain bees can push past that flap. On Bourbon, there were no such bees. Every year, the flowers had opened for a visitor who never came.

Edmond snapped a thin splinter off a bamboo stick. He slid it under the little flap and lifted it, gently, the way you lift the hand of a sleeping baby. Then he pressed the dusty cap down onto the sticky place with his thumb. He held it for a moment, and let go. The flower looked exactly the same as before. He did another, and another, until the sun was high and the flowers began to close.

For two days, nothing happened. The flowers he had touched wilted, like all the others. But they did not fall. On the third day, Edmond saw it. Where each of his flowers had been, a thin green finger was beginning to grow.

Bellier-Beaumont found them a week later. He stood very still in front of the vine. 'Who did this?' he asked. Edmond's heart was thumping. He had touched the old man's most precious plant without asking. 'I did,' he said. Bellier-Beaumont looked at him for a long moment. 'Show me,' he said.
So Edmond showed him. The splinter. The flap. The thumb.

After that, Edmond was taken from farm to farm across the island, to teach the enslaved workers how to do it. The farmers called it 'marrying' the vanilla. The green fingers took nine months to ripen into long pods. Then the pods were dried until they turned dark and sweet-smelling. Within a few years, the island was sending vanilla across the world.

Later, a well-known botanist said that he had taught Edmond the trick himself. Bellier-Beaumont wrote letters to say that this was not true, and that the boy had found it alone. In 1848, slavery ended on the island, and Edmond became free. He was given a new surname, Albius, from an old word for white, like the vanilla flower. But he was never paid for his idea, and he died poor, in 1880.

The vines did not forget him, though. Today, on farms in Madagascar, in Réunion, as Bourbon is now called, and in Kerala and Karnataka in India, people still walk along the vanilla vines in the early morning. They carry a thin stick. They lift the flap. They press with their thumb.

And when the pods are ripe, each one is packed with thousands of seeds, too small to see one at a time. If you have ever seen tiny black specks in a scoop of vanilla ice cream, you have seen them. Every speck is a seed. Every one began in a flower that opened for a single morning, and that someone, with a splinter and a thumb, helped to become a fruit.
story.epiphany: For the parent: a flower is not the end of a plant's work. It is where the fruit will grow, but only after pollen reaches the sticky place in its middle. The pumpkin flower that was dusted grew into a pumpkin. The one left alone shrivelled. The vanilla flowers had always been able to make fruit, but the insect that carries their pollen did not live on the island. Once Edmond moved the pollen himself, each flower turned into a pod full of seeds. That is the life cycle's turn from flower to fruit to seed. The story also asks who gets the credit for discoveries, and who does not.
ask: Why did the vanilla flowers drop off every year without making any pods?
What did Edmond learn from the two pumpkin flowers, the one that was dusted and the one left alone?
Edmond thought that a flower is 'a fruit that has not happened yet'. What did he mean?
A grown-up botanist said he had taught Edmond. Why do you think Bellier-Beaumont wrote letters to say it was not true?
The black specks in vanilla ice cream are seeds. What stage of the life cycle are they, and what could they become?

printables.title: 6 circle mats, one for each plant, each with 5 empty spaces joined by arrows

rules: Cut out the 30 stage cards and the 6 surprise cards. Shuffle them together into one pile, face down.
With 2 to 4 players: deal 5 cards to each player. Put the rest in a pile, face down, and turn the top card face up beside it.
On your turn, take one card: the top face-down card, or the face-up one. Then put one card face up on the discard pile. You must always have 5 cards.
You are trying to collect all 5 stages of one plant. When you have them, lay them on that plant's circle mat in the right order.
Then tell the life cycle out loud, starting from any stage, and say what comes after the fruit. If you get it right, you win.
If you pick up a surprise card, read it out and answer it. Then put it at the bottom of the pile and take another card.

Playing alone: lay all 36 cards face down in rows. Turn them over one at a time and put each stage card in its place on its plant's mat. Answer each surprise card. Time yourself. Next time, try to beat your time.
Playing alone, part two: ask someone, or the app, to hide one stage card. Find out which plant and which stage is missing.

flow.context: This is the first step of Time Detective. You set up a card game about putting plant life cycles back in order.
flow.do: 1. Cut out the cards and lay out the six circle mats. 2. Shuffle the stage cards and surprise cards together. 3. Deal 5 cards to each player, or lay them all face down if your child is playing alone.
flow.say: A storm has mixed up the life stories of six plants. We are detectives. We have to put each plant's life back in order, in a circle.
flow.kid: A storm mixed up six plants' life stories. You are the detective. Put each plant's stages back in a circle.

flow.do: Do one practice circle together with the moong cards, before the real game.
flow.say: Let's practise with moong. Which card comes after the seedling? And what comes after the fruit?
flow.kid: Practise with the moong cards. Put them in order. What comes after the fruit?

check.q: In a plant's life cycle, what comes after the fruit?
options: Nothing, the cycle has ended
New seeds, which start the cycle again
Another flower straight away
check.why: The fruit holds new seeds. Each seed can grow into a new plant, so the cycle starts again. That is why it is a circle, not a line. Picking 'nothing' usually means thinking of life as a line with an end. Picking 'another flower' misses the seed stage in between.

flow.do: Play the game by the rules. When a player lays down a full circle, they tell its life cycle aloud, starting from any stage.
flow.say: When you finish a circle, tell me the story. You can start anywhere. Start with the flower if you like.
flow.kid: Collect all five cards of one plant. Lay them in a circle. Tell their life story. You can start at any stage.
flow.parent: Good answers say what turns into what. 'The flower's base swells into the fruit. The fruit holds the seeds. Each seed grows into a seedling.' Starting from the flower or the fruit is a good sign. It shows the child sees a circle, not a line.

flow.do: Lay all six finished circles side by side. Compare them.
flow.say: Look at all six circles. Which plant takes the longest to go round? Which takes the shortest?
flow.kid: Look at all six circles. They have the same stages. Which plant goes round fastest? Which is slowest?

ask.q: What is the same about all six circles?
good: They all have seed, seedling, plant, flower and fruit.
They all go back to seeds.

flow.parent: Moong takes 2 to 3 months, rice about 4 months, bhindi, sunflower and pumpkin about 2 to 4 months. A mango tree takes 5 to 8 years to fruit for the first time, then fruits every year.
flow.think: Every circle has the same stages. So is a mango tree really so different from a moong plant?

check.q: The green cap on top of a brinjal is…
options: Left over from the brinjal's flower
A leaf that grew on the fruit later
A stalk added by the farmer
check.why: The green cap is made of the sepals, the small green leaves that wrapped the flower bud. They stay on while the flower's base swells into the brinjal. Picking 'a leaf that grew later' is a fair guess, because the cap is green like a leaf. But it was there before the fruit, around the flower.

worksheets.title: Round and Round: the plant life cycle (core)

items.p: A moong plant's life goes round in a circle. Put these stages in order, starting with the flower.
items.a: order shown
items.why: The flower grows into a pod. The pod holds seeds. A seed sprouts into a seedling, and the seedling grows into a grown plant, which makes flowers again. A cycle can start at any stage.

items.p: Saranya says a plant's life is a straight line, from a seed to the day the plant dies. Her friend Malar says it is a circle. Who is right? Explain.
items.a: Both have a point, but Malar is closer. One plant's life does end when they die. But before they die, they make seeds, and each seed can grow into a new plant that goes through the same stages. So the stages go round and round.
items.why: A strong answer agrees that one plant dies, and then explains that their seeds carry the stages on. That is why it is called a life cycle.

items.p: Which part of a flower swells up to become the fruit?
opts: The base in the very middle of the flower
items.why: The swollen base in the middle of the flower holds tiny seed-starts. It grows into the fruit, and the seed-starts become seeds. Picking 'the petals' is a common idea, because petals are the biggest, brightest part. But the petals fall off. The fruit grows from the middle.
items.art: A flower cut in half with its swollen middle base glowing.

items.p: To a scientist, which of these are fruits? Sort them.
cats: Fruit (grew from a flower, holds seeds)
items: Fruit (grew from a flower, holds seeds)
Fruit (grew from a flower, holds seeds)
Fruit (grew from a flower, holds seeds)
Fruit (grew from a flower, holds seeds)
items.a: see items
items.why: A fruit grows from a flower and holds seeds. Tomatoes, bhindi, chillies and pea pods all have seeds inside. A potato is a swollen stem, a carrot is a root and palak is a leaf.

items.p: Moving pollen from one flower to the middle of another flower is called ____.
items.why: Bees, butterflies, birds and the wind move pollen. Without pollination, most flowers fall off without making a fruit.

items.p: You tag a bhindi flower with a thread. Six days later, what will you most likely find on that spot?
items.why: A bhindi flower opens for one morning. Then its petals fall and its base grows into a pod, about a finger long after five or six days. Picking 'the same flower' means thinking flowers last a long time. Many last only a day. Some tagged flowers do fall off with no pod, which is normal.
items.context: In the Flower to Fruit experiment, you tie a loose thread around the stalk of an open flower, so you can find it again every day.

items.p: Match each stage to what happens in it.
pairs: waits, then sprouts when they get water, warmth and air
makes food in their leaves and gets big
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each stage has its own job. Together they make the whole circle.

items.p: A seedling's very first food comes from inside the seed.
items.why: True. A seed carries a store of food for the baby plant. Once their green leaves open, the seedling starts making their own food from air and water, using sunlight.

items.p: A plant that goes through their whole life cycle in one year or less, then dies, is called an ____.
items.why: Moong, rice and marigold are annuals. Plants that live for many years are called perennials.

items.p: Why do many plants make sweet, juicy fruits?
opts: So that the plant has something to eat
So that people can sell them
So that animals eat them and carry the seeds far away
items.why: Animals eat the fruit and drop or spit out the seeds somewhere else, where the new plant has more room. Picking 'so people can sell them' puts us at the centre. Plants made fruits for millions of years before there were people.

items.p: Name one fruit you ate this week. Where were its seeds? What part of its flower could you see on it?
items.a: Any honest answer. For example: I ate a tomato. Its seeds were in jelly in the middle. The green star on top was left from its flower.
items.why: Linking a real fruit to its seeds and its flower shows the child sees the life cycle in everyday food.

items.p: Draw the life cycle of a moong plant as a circle with arrows. Label each stage.
items.a: A circle with five or six stages joined by arrows: seed, seedling, grown plant, flower, pod, and back to seed.
items.why: A good drawing joins the last stage back to the first one. That is what makes it a cycle.

items.p: Gowri's family grows bhindi in a pot on their balcony. They disagree about when to pick the bhindi.

views.says: Pick every bhindi while they are young, about a finger long. Old bhindi are hard and stringy to eat.

views.who: Paati, Gowri's grandmother, who saves seeds
views.says: Leave a few pods on the plant until they turn dry and brown. Then we have seeds to sow next year.
If we pick them young, the plant makes more flowers. So we get more bhindi.

items.ask: What would you do with your bhindi plant? Give a reason from the life cycle. Then say one thing another person has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks a plan and explains it with the life cycle. For example: pick most pods young to eat, as Amma and Gowri say, but leave two or three to ripen for seeds, as Paati says. It explains that a ripe pod holds the seeds that start the next cycle.
items.why: There is a real trade-off. Young pods are best to eat, and picking them often makes the plant keep flowering. But only a pod left to ripen gives seeds for next year.

items.p: Thenmozhi finds a pumpkin flower with no tiny green ball behind the petals. Will this flower turn into a pumpkin?
opts: No. It is a male flower: it makes pollen, but no fruit
Yes, every flower becomes a fruit
items.why: A pumpkin plant has two kinds of flower. The female flower has a tiny green pumpkin behind the petals. The male flower has none, and only makes pollen. Picking 'if a bee visits' misses that there is nothing in this flower to grow into a pumpkin.

items.p: Cut a tomato across the middle. Draw what you see. Label the seeds, and the green star on top. What was the green star before the fruit grew?
items.a: A circle with seeds in jelly, in two or more parts. The green star is labelled 'sepals'. They wrapped the flower bud before it opened.
items.why: The tomato's seeds and their green star both show that the fruit was once a flower.
items.art: An empty box with a faint outline of a tomato cut in half.

items.p: Look at one plant in your home or on your street today. Which stage of their life cycle are they in? What clues tell you?
items.a: Any honest answer with a clue. For example: the tulsi on our balcony is a grown plant that is flowering, because they have thin purple flower spikes. Some spikes are dry and brown, so they may have seeds.
items.why: A strong answer names a stage and gives a clue the child really saw.

items.p: Look at the chart of a tagged bhindi pod. On which day was it 6 centimetres long?
items.why: Find 6 on the side of the chart, then follow it across to the line. The line reaches 6 above Day 4. Picking Day 6 usually means reading the last day instead of the matching point.
items.context: In the Flower to Fruit experiment, you tie a thread on an open bhindi flower's stalk. Every day you measure what grows there.

chart.title: Made-up example: length of a tagged bhindi pod, day by day
chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a bhindi pod often does. Your plant will be different.

items.p: The bhindi pod was 2 cm long on day 2 and 10 cm long on day 6. It grew ____ cm in those 4 days.
items.why: 10 take away 2 is 8. So it grew 8 cm in 4 days. That is about 2 cm a day.
items.context: In the Flower to Fruit experiment, you measure a young bhindi pod every day, from its stalk to its tip.

chart.title: Made-up example: length of a tagged bhindi pod, day by day
chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a bhindi pod often does. Your plant will be different.

items.p: Ammu tagged 10 brinjal flowers in a very hot week in May. Only 2 became brinjals. Her friend Farhan tagged 10 brinjal flowers in cool December, and 7 became brinjals. Give a reason for the difference.
items.a: In great heat, many plants drop their flowers, and pollen can stop working. Fewer insects may visit in the hottest hours too. In cool December the plant was not stressed, so more flowers got pollen and grew into fruits.
items.why: A strong answer links the season to the flower falling, and knows that a flower must get pollen to become a fruit.
items.context: In the Flower to Fruit experiment, you tie a loose thread around the stalk of an open flower, so you can find it again every day.

items.p: Altogether, the five pea pods had 6 + 7 + 5 + 8 + 6 = ____ peas.
items.context: In the Inside the Fruit experiment, you open pea pods and count the peas, which are the seeds.

chart.title: Made-up example: peas counted in five pea pods
chart.note: These numbers are made up. Your pods will be different.

items.p: A moong plant makes 20 pods. Each pod has about 10 seeds. About how many seeds does one plant give you?
items.why: 20 lots of 10 is 200. So one seed can give back about 200. Picking 30 means adding 20 and 10 instead of multiplying. There are 20 pods, and each one has 10 seeds.
items.context: In the Kitchen to Kitchen project, you grow moong from one seed all the way to new seeds, and count them.

items.p: Put these in order, from the shortest life cycle to the longest: mango, moong, neelakurinji, rice.
items.a: order shown
items.why: Moong takes 2 to 3 months, rice about 4 months, a mango tree 5 to 8 years before their first fruit, and neelakurinji 12 years to flower.

items.p: In the 1600s, van Helmont grew a willow tree in a pot for five years. The tree gained about 74 kilograms. The soil lost only about 57 grams. What does this show? What did van Helmont himself get wrong?
items.a: It shows that the tree's body did not come from the soil, because the soil hardly changed. Van Helmont decided the tree was made from water alone. He missed the air. Most of a tree's dry body is built from carbon dioxide in the air, joined with water using sunlight.
items.why: A strong answer uses the numbers as evidence, then says that water was only part of the answer. Most people today still guess 'the soil'.

items.p: Indu does the Floating Leaves test again, but forgets the pinch of baking soda. In bright light, hardly any leaf circles float. Why?
opts: Baking soda gives the water carbon dioxide, which the leaf needs to make food and oxygen
items.why: To make food, a leaf needs carbon dioxide as well as light. Baking soda gives off carbon dioxide into the water. Without it, the leaf can make very little oxygen, so few bubbles lift the circles. Picking 'makes leaves lighter' misses that the bubbles are what lift them.
items.context: In the Floating Leaves experiment, you push the air out of small circles of palak leaf so they sink, in water with a pinch of baking soda. Then you watch them in bright light.

items.p: Match each plant to how a new plant can grow without a seed.
pairs: from the eyes on the potato
from the bulb's bottom in water or soil
from a stem cutting in water
from a shoot at the base of the old plant
from baby plants on the edges of their leaves
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each of these grows a copy of themselves from one of their own parts. A new plant grown this way is a clone of their parent.

items.p: A moong plant dies after their pods ripen.
items.why: True. Moong is an annual. They finish their life cycle in two to three months. Their seeds carry the cycle on.

items.p: Why do farmers in Réunion and in Kerala move vanilla pollen by hand?
opts: The insect that carries vanilla pollen in Mexico does not live there
items.why: In Mexico, certain bees are thought to push past the little flap inside the vanilla flower. Those bees do not live in other countries. So people do the bees' job with a thin stick and a thumb. Picking 'no pollen' misses the point of the story: the pollen was always there, hidden behind the flap.
items.context: In this unit's story, Edmond, a 12-year-old boy on an island in the Indian Ocean, finds out how to make vanilla flowers grow pods in 1841.

items.p: A green chilli plant in a pot makes lots of flowers, but no chillies. Give two reasons why that might happen, and one thing to try.
items.a: For example: no insects visit the balcony, so pollen does not reach the flowers. Or it is too hot, or the pot dried out. I could gently shake the flowers in the morning, or move pollen with a soft brush, and water them regularly.
items.why: A flower needs pollen to become a fruit, and a plant drops flowers when they are stressed by heat or thirst.

items.p: Which of these plants flower only once in their whole life, and then die?
opts: The bamboo in Mizoram that flowers after about 48 years
items.why: That bamboo grows for about 48 years, flowers once, makes their seeds and dies. Mango, neem and rose are perennials that flower again and again. Picking mango may come from knowing mango trees take years to fruit. But once they start, they fruit every year.

items.p: Write the life cycle of a mango tree as a short story, in 5 sentences. Start with a ripe mango falling to the ground.
items.a: For example: A ripe mango fell to the ground. A monkey ate it and dropped the stone far away. In the rains the stone sprouted into a seedling with red leaves. After six years the seedling was a big tree and made tiny flowers. The flowers turned into mangoes, with new stones inside.
items.why: Starting with the fruit shows the child understands that a cycle can start at any stage.

items.p: The neem tree outside Shanthi's building drops hundreds of fruits every year. Almost none of them grow into new trees.

views.says: The tree wastes almost all their fruits. Making so many is pointless.
Nothing is wasted. Birds and squirrels eat the fruits, and the fallen ones rot and feed the soil.

views.who: A botanist, a scientist who studies plants
views.says: Making many seeds is how a tree makes sure that a few of them land in a good place and grow.

items.ask: Is the neem tree wasteful? Pick a side and give your evidence. Then answer back from another side.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side with evidence. For Shanthi: each fruit costs the tree food to make, and most never grow. For the grandmother: the fruits feed birds, and their atoms go back to the soil for other plants. For the botanist: most seeds fail, so a tree that makes many seeds is more likely to have a few young trees. A strong answer then gives another side its due.
items.why: This is a real trade-off. Fruits cost a tree a lot to make, but most seeds never find a good place to grow. Many plants make huge numbers of seeds, and the fruits that don't grow still feed other living beings.

items.p: Draw a bar chart of how long these plants take to go from sowing a seed to their first new seeds: moong 3 months, rice 4 months, tomato 4 months, papaya 10 months. Label the bottom line and the side line.
items.a: Four bars. Moong 3 squares, rice 4, tomato 4, papaya 10. The bottom line says 'Plant' and the side line says 'Months'.
items.why: A bar chart shows at a glance that papaya takes much longer than the others. The times are rounded, and real plants vary with the weather.
items.art: Empty squared graph paper with a bottom line and a side line numbered 0 to 12.

worksheets.title: Life Cycle Puzzles and Big Ideas (challenge)

items.p: In 1938, scientists flashed a light in the middle of the night on plants that flower when nights are long. The plants did not flower. What does this tell us?
opts: The light made the night warmer
The plants were measuring the length of the dark night, and the light broke it into two short nights
items.why: The plants count how long the dark lasts. One flash cut the long night into two short ones, so the plants sensed two short nights instead of one long one. Picking 'the light hurt the plants' is a careful guess. But the plants kept growing healthy leaves. They just did not flower.
items.context: Many plants flower only at a certain time of year. Scientists wanted to know how they tell the season.

items.p: A mango tree with very sweet mangoes is growing in your garden. You plant one of their mango stones. Will the new tree have exactly the same sweet mangoes?
opts: Not always, because the seed got some of their instructions from the pollen of another tree
Only if you water them with sugar
items.why: Each seed gets instructions from both parents, so they can be a little different. That is why farmers grow their best mangoes by joining a twig of the sweet tree onto a young tree. This makes a copy. Picking 'yes, always' is a natural guess, since a mango seed always grows a mango tree. But the mangoes on the new tree can be different.

items.p: When a big tree burns, only a small heap of ash is left. Where did the rest of the tree go? What does this tell you about what the tree was made of?
items.a: Most of the tree went back into the air, as carbon dioxide and water vapour. The ash is the small part that came from the soil, the minerals. This shows the tree was built mostly from air and water, and burning sends it back there.
items.why: A strong answer says the wood did not vanish. The wood changed into gases. Matter cannot disappear. It changes form.

items.p: Chillies are hot to mice but not to birds. How does this help the chilli plant?
opts: It does not help at all
Mice chew up the seeds, but birds swallow them whole and drop them far away
items.why: In 2001, scientists found that the heat keeps away mammals, which chew the seeds. The hot taste does not burn birds, so they eat the chillies and carry the seeds far away. Picking 'birds like spicy food' misses the point. Birds do not taste the burn at all.

items.p: Plants live their lives in very different ways. Imagine three of them could speak.

views.says: I live fast. In about 3 months I make around 200 seeds, before the dry season comes.
I take years to make my first fruit. But then I fruit every summer for a hundred years.
I wait about 48 years and flower once, all at the same time as my neighbours. Then I die.

items.ask: Which way of living would work best in a place with a long dry season every year? Pick one and give your reasons. Then say what another plant's way does well.
items.a: A strong answer uses the life cycle. For moong: the plant finishes before the dry season, and the dry seeds wait safely for the rain. For mango: deep roots can reach water, and a big tree survives many dry seasons. A strong answer then gives another way its due. For bamboo, flowering all together makes so many seeds that animals cannot eat them all. Scientists think this may be why.
items.why: Every way works somewhere. A short life suits a short wet season. A long life suits a plant that can survive bad years. The bamboo's reason is still being studied.

items.p: Neelakurinji bloomed near Munnar in 2018. They bloom every 12 years. Their next two blooms should be in ____ and ____.
In the 1950s, a disease wiped out most of the world's favourite banana, the Gros Michel. Why did it spread through so many farms?
opts: All the plants were copies of each other, so they all had the same weakness
items.why: Bananas are grown from shoots, so the plants are clones. A disease that can harm one can harm them all. Picking 'too much rain' is a sensible guess about plant diseases. But the real problem was that there was no difference between the plants.

items.p: Every kind of plant makes flowers and seeds.
items.why: False. Ferns and mosses have no flowers and no seeds. Ferns spread by spores, a fine dust made under their leaves. Ferns are much older than flowering plants.

items.p: Your food comes from plants. Plants are built mostly from air. Explain, step by step, how some of the air could end up in your body.
items.a: A rice leaf takes in carbon dioxide from the air. It uses sunlight to make sugar, and stores some as starch in the rice grain. The rice is ground into batter and steamed into an idli. I eat the idli, and my body uses the carbon in it to build itself.
items.why: This follows a carbon atom through photosynthesis and food. It is a real path that carbon atoms take every day.

items.p: In the Be Edmond experiment, you cover one pumpkin flower with a bag and add no pollen. It shrivels. You cover another with a bag and add pollen by hand. It grows. Why do you cover BOTH with bags?
opts: So that the bag is the same for both, and only the pollen is different
items.why: In a fair test, only one thing changes. If only one flower had a bag, you could not tell whether the bag or the pollen made the difference. Picking 'bags make fruits grow' is the opposite of what the bagged, unpollinated flower shows.
items.context: In the Be Edmond experiment, you move pollen by hand from a male flower to a female flower on a pumpkin, gourd or cucumber vine.

items.p: Is a seed a new plant, or the old plant carrying on? Give one reason for each answer.
items.a: A balanced answer. For example: they are new, because they are a separate living thing and may be a bit different from their parent. They are the old plant carrying on, because they carry copied instructions and were fed with their parent's food.
items.why: Scientists and thinkers answer this in different ways. What counts is a reason for each side.

items.p: In 1982, small thale cress plants on a space station flowered and made seeds. Why was that important?
opts: It showed plants grow better in space
It showed a plant can go round their whole life cycle in space
It showed plants do not need water
items.why: People living far from Earth will need plants that can make new seeds there, again and again. Picking 'plants grow better in space' is not what was found. Growing plants in space is hard.

items.p: Charles Darwin called the fast spread of flowering plants 'an abominable mystery'. Give two ideas scientists have for why flowering plants spread so fast.
items.a: Any two of these. Flowers changed together with the insects and birds that move their pollen. Flowering plants finish their life cycles quickly. Fruits let animals carry seeds far away. Changes in the climate helped them.
items.why: Scientists still argue about this. A good answer gives two different ideas.
items.context: The first flowering plants appeared about 130 million years ago. Today almost 9 in every 10 kinds of land plant have flowers.

items.p: Draw the life cycle of a moong plant inside a bigger circle that shows where their atoms come from and go to: air, water, soil, and decomposers.
items.a: An inner circle of seed, seedling, plant, flower, pod and seed. Around it, arrows from the air and the soil into the plant, and arrows from the dead plant through decomposers back to the air and soil.
items.why: A plant's life cycle sits inside a bigger cycle of atoms going round through air, soil and living things.

items.p: Big trees grow from big seeds, and small plants grow from small seeds.
items.why: False. A banyan tree, one of the biggest trees in India, grows from a seed about as small as a mustard seed. A coconut is a huge seed, but a coconut palm is far smaller than a big banyan. Seed size does not tell you how big the plant will be.

items.p: Sort these. Did each one need pollen to reach a flower first?
items: a new potato plant from an eye
a money plant from a cutting
a pea pod full of peas
a banana shoot at the base of the old plant
items.a: see items
items.why: A fruit with seeds grows only after pollen reaches a flower. A new plant grown from a part of the old plant, like an eye, a cutting or a shoot, needs no flower and no pollen.

experiments.title: Flower to Fruit: tag a flower and watch it change
experiments.context: In this experiment you tie a thread on the stalk of a flower that has just opened. Then you visit it every day, to see what the flower turns into.
experiments.question: What happens to a flower after it opens? Does every flower turn into a fruit?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess two things. How many of your 5 tagged flowers will turn into fruits? And on which day will you first see a baby fruit? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: This is a watching test, so keep the watching the same. Tag flowers that opened on the same morning, on the same plant. Check them at the same time every day. Measure each one the same way, from where it joins its stalk to its tip. Treat the tagged flowers just like the rest of the plant.

materials.item: a plant that has flowers and some fruits on it now: bhindi, brinjal, chilli, tomato, a gourd vine or a lemon tree. A potted chilli or brinjal from a nursery works well
5 short pieces of coloured thread or wool, each about as long as your hand
a ruler
a notebook and pencil

experiments.safety: Wash your hands after touching the plant. After touching a chilli plant, do not rub your eyes. Watch out for ants and bees, and leave them alone.

Check each tagged flower. Draw it. Did the petals fall?
Check, measure and draw.
Check, measure and draw.
Check, measure and draw.
Check, measure and draw. Compare the flowers.
Check, measure and draw.
Check, measure and draw.
Check, measure and draw.
Count how many flowers became fruits. Draw a line graph of one fruit's length. Say what you think, what you saw and why.

experiments.record: Fill in the table for each flower. Draw one tagged flower every day, on the same page, in a row. Then draw a line graph of one fruit's length, day by day.
