example_chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a bhindi pod often does. Your plant will be different.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Flower to Fruit experiment. You look closely at one plant that has flowers and fruits on it at the same time.
flow.do: 1. Stand by the plant with your child. 2. Together, find a tight bud, an open flower, a wilted flower, a tiny fruit and a big fruit. 3. Ask your child to put them in order, youngest first.
flow.say: This one plant is showing us several stages at once. Find a bud, an open flower, an old flower, a baby fruit and a big fruit. Which do you think is youngest?
flow.kid: Look at the whole plant. Find a bud and an open flower. Find an old flower, a baby fruit and a big fruit. Which is the youngest?

ask.q: How do you think the baby fruit got there?
good: There was a flower there before.

flow.parent: On bhindi, brinjal, chilli and tomato you can usually see every stage at once. If you have no flowering plant, a nursery sells potted chilli or brinjal plants that are already flowering. Or ask a neighbour if you may visit their plant every day.

flow.do: 1. Choose 5 flowers that opened this morning. If fewer than 5 opened today, tag more over the next two days. Write down the day you tagged each one. 2. Tie a different coloured thread loosely round each flower's stalk, just below the flower. Leave room, because the stalk will get thicker. 3. Write the colours in the table. 4. Ask your child to guess how many will become fruits.
flow.say: Let's tag five flowers that opened today. A thread on each stalk, loose, not tight. Now guess. How many will turn into fruits?
flow.kid: Pick 5 flowers that opened today. Tie a thread loosely round each stalk. Write down the colours. Guess: how many will become fruits?
flow.parent: Most flowers open in the morning. Bhindi flowers close by the afternoon, so tag them early. Tie the thread on the flower's own short stalk, not on the main stem. Otherwise you will not know which flower it was.

flow.wait: Every day for 8 days, about 3 minutes
flow.do: Each day, at about the same time: 1. Find each thread. 2. Look at what is there now. 3. Measure any baby fruit from where it joins the stalk to its tip. 4. Draw one of them, and write the numbers in the table.
flow.say: What has changed since yesterday? Are the petals still there? Is anything growing in the middle?
flow.kid: Visit your threads. What has changed? Measure any baby fruit. Draw one. Write the numbers down.
flow.parent: What to expect. Bhindi: the petals fall the next day and a pod is about a finger long by day 5 or 6. Chilli and brinjal: a small fruit shows in about 5 to 7 days. Tomato: a pea-sized green ball by about day 7, and it takes weeks to ripen. Some tagged flowers will dry and drop off with no fruit. That is normal, and it is a real result. It happens more in very hot or very dry weather, or where few insects visit. In cold weather everything is slower, so give it up to 14 days.

flow.do: On about day 6, line up your drawings and compare the flowers.
flow.say: Look at your drawings in a row. Where did the fruit come from?
flow.kid: Put your drawings in a row. Where did the fruit come from?

check.q: Your tagged flower's petals fell off, and a little fruit grew in the same place. Which part of the flower became the fruit?
options: The petals
The middle part, at the base of the flower
The thread made it grow
check.why: The petals fall off, but the swollen base in the middle of the flower stays and grows into the fruit. Picking 'the petals' is a common idea, because they are the biggest part of a flower. But they drop away. The fruit was hiding in the middle all along.

flow.do: 1. On day 10, count how many of the 5 flowers became fruits. 2. Help your child draw a line graph of one fruit's length. Put the days along the bottom and the length up the side. 3. If a grown-up picks one young fruit and cuts it open, look for the tiny seeds inside.
flow.say: Let's turn the numbers into a line. Each dot is one day's length. Join the dots. Does the line go up slowly or quickly?
flow.kid: Count: how many flowers became fruits? Draw a dot for each day's length. Join the dots. Look for seeds inside a fruit.
flow.parent: Cutting the fruit is for a grown-up. A young bhindi pod has rows of soft white seeds. A young chilli has pale seeds round its middle. These seeds came from tiny seed-starts in the flower.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Now tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: a flower turns into a fruit, but not every flower does. What I saw: the petals fell off the next day. The middle grew into a bhindi pod 10 cm long by day 6. Three of my five flowers became pods, and two fell off. Why: the base of the flower swells into the fruit. That happens if pollen reached it and the plant has enough water.

experiments.title: Inside the Fruit: find the seeds and the flower's leftovers
experiments.context: In this experiment you take fruits from your kitchen, find what is left of their flowers on the outside, and open them to count the seeds inside.
experiments.question: Does every fruit hold seeds? And can you find the flower each fruit came from?
experiments.predict: Before cutting, guess which fruit will have the most seeds. Write your guess for each fruit in the table. Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Treat every fruit the same way. Look at the outside first, then cut each one across the middle. Count the seeds the same way each time. If a fruit has too many to count, count one part and multiply. Write in the table which ones you worked out that way.

materials.item: 4 or 5 kitchen fruits, for example a tomato, a bhindi, a pea pod or a green chilli, a cucumber or a brinjal, and a banana
a knife and a chopping board, for a grown-up
a plate and a spoon
a magnifying glass, if you have one
the results table and a pencil

experiments.safety: Only a grown-up uses the knife. If you open a chilli, wash your hands straight after and do not touch your eyes.

schedule.what: Find the flower leftovers, open each fruit, and count the seeds.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw one fruit cut open, with its seeds, and label where its flower used to be.

setup.caption: 2. A grown-up cuts each fruit across the middle.

Green star, and a tiny dot at the bottom

flow.context: This is the first step of the Inside the Fruit experiment. You look at the outside of kitchen fruits for leftover parts of their flowers.
flow.do: 1. Put the fruits on a plate. 2. Look at each one all over, before cutting. 3. Help your child find the leftovers of each flower. 4. Ask them to guess how many seeds are in each fruit, and write the guesses down.
flow.say: Every one of these was once a flower. Let's look for clues. Can you find anything left over from the flower?
flow.kid: Every fruit here was once a flower. Look all over each one. Can you find a leftover flower part? Guess how many seeds are inside.

ask.q: What do you think the green star on the tomato was?
good: The green bits that wrapped the bud.

flow.parent: Clues to find: the tomato's green star and the brinjal's green cap are the sepals that wrapped the bud. A tomato also has a tiny dot at the bottom, where the middle of the flower was. A banana's dark tip, and a young cucumber's dry tip, are where the flower was. A pea pod has green sepals at its stalk end, and a pointed tip where the middle of the flower was.

flow.do: Cut each fruit across the middle. Show your child how the seeds are arranged inside.
flow.say: Look how the seeds are arranged. The bhindi has rows, like a star. The tomato has little rooms full of jelly.
flow.kid: Ask a grown-up to cut each fruit across the middle. Look at the seeds. Are they in rows, rooms or a ring?
flow.parent: A bhindi cut across shows about 5 rows of seeds, like a star. A tomato has 2 to 4 rooms of jelly with seeds in it. A cucumber has 3 parts. A banana shows only a ring of tiny black specks.

flow.do: 1. Count all the seeds in small fruits, like a pea pod. 2. For a bhindi, split it along its length and count the seeds in one row. Then multiply by the number of rows. 3. For a tomato, squeeze one room onto a plate, spread it with a spoon and count. Then multiply by the number of rooms.
flow.say: This tomato has too many seeds to count one by one. Let's count one room and multiply. Scientists do this too.
flow.kid: Count the seeds in the pea pod. For a bhindi, count one row. Then multiply by the number of rows. Write each number down.
flow.parent: Rough numbers to expect: 4 to 9 in a pea pod, 40 to 80 in a bhindi, and 50 to 150 in a small tomato. Your numbers will be different, and that is fine.

check.q: A banana has only tiny black specks, and no real seeds. Why?
options: Someone took the seeds out
Bananas are not fruits
The bananas we eat are a kind that grows fruit without real seeds
check.why: Wild bananas are full of hard seeds. The bananas we eat are a kind that grows fruit without real seeds. The black specks are seed-starts that never grew. Farmers grow new banana plants from shoots instead. Picking 'not fruits' is a fair guess. But a banana still grows from a flower, so it is a fruit.

flow.do: Compare the guesses with the counts.
flow.say: Which fruit had the most seeds? The fewest? Each seed came from one tiny seed-start in the flower.
flow.kid: Which fruit had the most seeds? Were your guesses close? Each seed was once a tiny seed-start in the flower.
flow.think: A papaya has hundreds of seeds. A mango has just one. Why might a plant make so many, or so few?

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Now tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: fruits hold seeds, and they grow from flowers. What I saw: the pea pod had 6 seeds and the bhindi about 60. The tomato still had a green star from its flower. Why: the base of each flower swelled into the fruit, and its tiny seed-starts grew into seeds.

experiments.title: Be Edmond: help a pumpkin flower become a fruit
experiments.context: In this unit's story, a boy named Edmond moves pollen by hand to make flowers grow fruit. In this experiment you do the same on a pumpkin, gourd or cucumber vine, and test whether a flower needs pollen to make a fruit.
experiments.question: Does a female flower need pollen to grow into a fruit?
experiments.predict: Guess first. You will have three female flowers. One is left open for insects. One is covered with a bag and gets no pollen. One is covered with a bag and gets pollen from you. Which will grow into fruits? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use female flowers on the same vine that open on the same morning, or as close together as you can. Cover two of them with a bag the evening before they open, so no insect can get in first. Give pollen to only one of the covered flowers. The bag is the same for both covered flowers, so only the pollen is different.

materials.item: a vine with big flowers: pumpkin, cucumber, karela, lauki, tori, tinda or watermelon. A terrace garden, a farm or a neighbour's vine is fine
2 small paper bags, or 2 squares of old net or thin cloth, and some thread
a soft paintbrush or a cotton bud
3 coloured threads, to tell the flowers apart

experiments.safety: Do this with a grown-up near the vine. Watch for bees, and move away slowly if one comes. Wash your hands afterwards.

schedule.what: In the evening, find three female-flower buds about to open. Cover two with bags. Tag all three.
Early in the morning, move pollen from a male flower to one covered flower. Cover it again.
Take the bags off. Check all three baby fruits.
Check: which baby fruits are growing, and which are going yellow?
Compare all three. Say what you think, what you saw and why.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw the three baby fruits on day 4, side by side.

setup.art: Two pumpkin flowers side by side, one with a tiny green pumpkin behind its petals labelled as a female flower, one on a thin stalk labelled as a male flower.
setup.caption: 1. Find female flowers, with a baby fruit behind, and male flowers.

setup.art: A small paper bag tied loosely with thread over a closed pumpkin flower bud on the vine, in the evening.
setup.caption: 2. The evening before, cover two female buds with bags.

setup.art: A child brushing yellow pollen from a male flower onto the sticky middle of an open female flower, early in the morning.
setup.caption: 3. In the morning, brush pollen into one covered flower. Cover it again.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Be Edmond experiment. You learn to tell a vine's female flowers from their male flowers.
flow.do: 1. Look along the vine together. 2. Find a female flower: it has a tiny baby fruit behind its petals. 3. Find a male flower: it is on a thin stalk, with no baby fruit behind it.
flow.say: These flowers look alike from the front. Turn them over. The female flower has a tiny fruit behind it. The male flower has only pollen. In the story, they were called mother and father flowers.
flow.kid: Look behind each flower. A tiny fruit behind it? That is a female flower. No fruit, on a thin stalk? That is a male flower.
flow.parent: A young vine often makes only male flowers for the first week or two. Female flowers come later, and there are fewer of them. Pumpkin, cucumber and karela flowers open early in the morning, about 6 to 9 o'clock, and close by midday. Lauki flowers are white and tori flowers are yellow. Both open in the evening, so do this experiment at dusk with them.

flow.do: 1. In the evening, find three female-flower buds that will open tomorrow. They are big, and their tips are turning yellow or white. 2. Tie a thread on each stalk: red, blue and green. 3. Cover the blue one and the green one with a paper bag or net, tied loosely round the stalk. 4. Leave the red one uncovered.
flow.say: The bag stops any insect getting in first. The red flower stays open, so insects can visit it.
flow.kid: Find three female buds that will open tomorrow. Tie a thread on each. Cover two with bags. Leave one open.

flow.do: 1. Next morning, pick a fresh, open male flower. 2. Peel back its petals and touch the middle: yellow dust should come off on your finger. 3. Pick up the dust with the paintbrush or cotton bud. Or use the male flower itself, like a brush. 4. Open the green flower's bag. Brush the pollen gently all over the sticky middle of the female flower. 5. Close the bag again. 6. Do not touch the blue flower.
flow.say: Now we do what Edmond did. We carry the pollen ourselves. Gently, like painting with the softest brush.
flow.kid: Pick a male flower. Peel back its petals. See the yellow dust? Pick it up with the brush. Open the green flower's bag. Brush the dust gently into its middle. Close the bag.
flow.parent: Do this early, before about 10 o'clock for morning flowers, while the flowers are fresh. If no dust comes off on your finger, try a different male flower that opened this morning.

flow.wait: Check once a day for 3 days
flow.do: 1. On day 3, take the bags off, because the flowers have closed. 2. Each day, look at the three baby fruits behind the old flowers. Are they green and growing, or yellow and soft?
flow.say: Which baby fruits are growing? Which are going yellow?
flow.kid: Take the bags off. Check the three baby fruits each day. Green and growing? Or yellow and soft?
flow.parent: A female flower that got pollen usually stays green and starts to swell within 2 or 3 days. One that got none goes yellow and soft, and drops off within 2 to 5 days. The open flower grows only if an insect visited it. In very hot weather, even pollinated flowers sometimes drop. If that happens, try again: a vine in season makes new flowers almost every day.

check.q: The covered flower with no pollen went yellow and fell off. The covered flower with pollen grew. What does that show?
options: Yellow flowers never make fruit
A female flower needs pollen to grow into a fruit
Bags stop fruits growing
check.why: Both flowers had bags, so the bag was the same. Only the pollen was different. The one with pollen grew, so the pollen made the difference. Picking 'bags stop fruits growing' cannot be right, because the bagged flower with pollen grew too.

flow.do: Compare all three flowers on day 5.
flow.say: Edmond found out that vanilla flowers needed someone to carry their pollen. Who carried pollen to our red flower?
flow.kid: Compare your three flowers. Who carried pollen to the open red flower? Edmond did this job for vanilla flowers!
flow.think: Bees, butterflies, moths and even bats carry pollen for free. What would happen to our food if they all disappeared?

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Now tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: a female pumpkin flower needs pollen to become a pumpkin. What I saw: the covered flower with no pollen went yellow and fell off on day 3. The covered flower I brushed with pollen was twice as big by day 4. Why: the pollen has to reach the middle of the flower. Only then can its base grow into a fruit with seeds.

experiments.title: Floating Leaves: does a leaf make gas in the light?
experiments.context: In this experiment you make small circles of palak leaf sink in a glass of water. Then you watch whether they float back up in bright light and in the dark. It shows a leaf using light to make food and oxygen, the way a growing plant feeds themselves.
experiments.question: Do leaves make gas when light shines on them?
experiments.predict: Guess first. The leaf circles will sink to the bottom of two glasses. One glass goes in bright light and one in a dark cupboard. In which glass will the circles float up? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Make the two glasses the same. Use the same water, the same pinch of baking soda and drop of soap, and 10 circles cut from the same leaf in each. Change only the light. Count the floating circles in both glasses at the same times.
results_table: Glass in bright light: circles floating
Glass in the dark: circles floating

materials.item: 2 or 3 fresh palak leaves
a paper or plastic drinking straw, to cut out leaf circles
a 10 ml plastic syringe with no needle, from a chemist
baking soda, also called meetha soda: a small pinch for each glass
washing-up liquid: one tiny drop for each glass
2 clear glasses, each half full of tap water
bright sunlight at a window, or a bright lamp
a clock or a phone timer

experiments.safety: The syringe has no needle. Do not drink the water. Wash the glasses well afterwards.

schedule.what: Sink the leaf circles, then count how many float in the light and in the dark.

experiments.record: Fill in the table every 5 minutes. Then draw a bar for each glass, showing how many circles were floating after 20 minutes.

setup.art: A drinking straw pressed down onto a palak leaf on a fingertip, cutting out a small green circle.
setup.caption: 1. Press a straw into a palak leaf to cut 20 small circles.

setup.art: Leaf circles inside a plastic syringe with water, a finger covering the tip while the plunger is pulled back.
setup.caption: 2. In the syringe, block the tip and pull the plunger. The circles sink.

setup.art: Two glasses of water: one in bright sunshine with green circles floating at the top, one in a dark cupboard with circles still at the bottom.
setup.caption: 3. One glass in bright light, one in the dark. Count the floaters.

example_chart.title: Made-up example: leaf circles floating after 20 minutes (out of 10 in each glass)
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what often happens. Your numbers will be different.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Floating Leaves experiment. You make water with extra carbon dioxide in it, for the leaves to use.
flow.do: 1. Half fill two clear glasses with tap water. 2. Add a small pinch of baking soda to each, about an eighth of a teaspoon. 3. Add one tiny drop of washing-up liquid to each. 4. Stir gently, so it does not foam.
flow.say: Baking soda puts extra carbon dioxide in the water. That is the gas leaves use to make food. The drop of soap helps the water soak into the leaf.
flow.kid: Half fill two glasses with water. Add a small pinch of baking soda to each. Add one tiny drop of soap. Stir gently.

flow.do: 1. Lay a palak leaf on a soft eraser or your fingertip. 2. Press the straw straight down and twist, to cut out a circle. 3. Cut 20 circles. Try to miss the thick veins.
flow.say: We need 20 little leaf circles, 10 for each glass.
flow.kid: Press the straw into the leaf and twist. Out pops a circle! Cut 20. Miss the thick lines in the leaf.

flow.do: 1. Pull the plunger out of the syringe. Drop 10 circles in. 2. Push the plunger back in gently, without squashing them. 3. Suck up water from one glass until the syringe is half full. 4. Point it up and push out the air. 5. Cover the tip firmly with a finger. Pull the plunger back hard and hold for 10 seconds, then let go. 6. Do this 3 to 5 times, until the circles sink.
flow.say: Pulling the plunger sucks the air out of the leaf circles. Water goes in instead, so they sink. Leaves have air spaces inside, like a sponge.
flow.kid: Put 10 circles in the syringe. Suck up some water. Push out the air. Block the tip with a finger. Pull the plunger back hard. Do it again until they sink.
flow.parent: Your child can do most of this, but small hands may need help holding the tip shut while pulling. Will the circles not sink after 5 tries? Add one more tiny drop of soap to the water and try again.

flow.do: 1. Squirt the sunk circles into the first glass. 2. Do the same with 10 more circles for the second glass. 3. If any circle floats, poke it down or sink it again.
flow.say: All 20 circles are at the bottom now. Let's give them different places to wait.
flow.kid: Squirt the circles into the first glass. Do 10 more for the second glass. Are they all at the bottom?

flow.do: 1. Put one glass in bright sunlight, or close under a bright lamp. 2. Put the other in a dark cupboard. 3. Every 5 minutes, count the floating circles in each glass and write the numbers in the table.
flow.say: Every five minutes, let's count. Look closely at the circles in the light. Can you see tiny bubbles?
flow.kid: One glass in bright light. One in the dark cupboard. Every 5 minutes, count the floaters. Write the numbers. Look for tiny bubbles.
flow.parent: In strong sunlight the first circles usually rise after about 5 to 15 minutes. Most float within 20 to 25 minutes. Under a weak lamp or on a cloudy day it is slower, so move the lamp closer or wait longer. The circles in the dark usually stay down. While you wait, your child can draw the two glasses.

check.q: Why did the leaf circles in the light float up?
options: The leaves made oxygen gas while making food, and the tiny bubbles lifted them
The light pushed them up
The water in the light was different
check.why: In light, the leaf circles take in carbon dioxide and make sugar, giving out oxygen. Tiny bubbles of oxygen fill the spaces inside them, like little floats. In the dark they cannot do this. Picking 'the water was different' would break our fair test. Both glasses had the same water, so only the light was different.

flow.do: Swap the glasses: put the dark glass in the light, and the light glass in the dark. Look again in 15 minutes.
flow.say: What do you think will happen now?
flow.kid: Swap the two glasses. What will happen now? Look again later.
flow.parent: The dark circles now usually float too. The floating ones put in the dark slowly sink again over 20 to 30 minutes. The leaf uses up its oxygen to breathe.
flow.think: A whole tree is doing this in the sun, all day. Where does the oxygen go?

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Now tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: leaves make gas when light shines on them. What I saw: after 20 minutes, 9 circles were floating in the light, and none in the dark. Why: in light, the leaf makes food from carbon dioxide and water, and gives out oxygen. The bubbles of oxygen lifted the circles.

activities.title: The Life Cycle Hunt
activities.context: This is a hunt around your home and street. You look for plants at every stage of their life cycle: seeds, seedlings, grown plants, buds, flowers, fruits and dry seeds.

materials.item: a hunt card: a sheet of paper with 8 boxes labelled seed, seedling, grown plant, bud, open flower, old flower, fruit, dry seeds
a pencil, or a phone to take photos

activities.safety: Go outside only with a grown-up. Look and draw, but do not pick plants that are not yours.

schedule.what: Hunt for every life cycle stage, at home and on a short walk.

activities.record: Draw or photograph one thing in each box of the hunt card. Write where you found it.

setup.art: A hunt card with 8 empty boxes, each with a small symbol: a seed, a sprout, a plant, a bud, a flower, a wilted flower, a fruit, dry seeds.
setup.caption: 1. Make a hunt card with 8 boxes.

setup.art: A child and a parent on a street looking at a hibiscus bush with buds, open flowers and old wilted flowers.
setup.caption: 2. Hunt at home and on a walk. Look for every stage.

setup.art: A child drawing a lemon tree that has flowers and small green lemons at the same time.
setup.caption: 3. Bonus: find one plant showing three stages at once.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Life Cycle Hunt. You make a card with a box for each stage of a plant's life.
flow.do: 1. Help your child draw 8 boxes on a sheet. 2. Label them: seed, seedling, grown plant, bud, open flower, old flower, fruit, dry seeds.
flow.say: We are going to find every stage of a plant's life, today, near our home. Can we fill all 8 boxes?
flow.kid: Draw 8 boxes on your paper. Label them with the stages. Can you find all 8 today?

flow.do: 1. Start in the kitchen: seeds are easy there. 2. Look at pot plants on the balcony or windowsill. 3. Go for a short walk. Look at road edges, cracks in walls, gardens and the vegetable cart.
flow.say: Where could a seedling be hiding? Look in cracks, at the edge of the road and under trees.
flow.kid: Start in the kitchen. Then look at pot plants. Then go outside with a grown-up. Fill each box.
flow.parent: Good finds: dal and jeera in the kitchen, and seedlings in wall cracks or under a neem tree. Look for hibiscus or rose buds, grass with seed heads, and the vegetable cart full of fruits. A lemon tree, a chilli plant or a bhindi plant often shows flowers and fruits at the same time.

flow.do: Look at the finished card together.
flow.say: Which box was hardest to fill? Did you find one plant with three stages at once?
flow.kid: Which box was hardest to fill? Did one plant show three stages at once?

check.q: You find a lemon tree with flowers and small green lemons on it at the same time. What does this show?
options: The tree is sick
Lemons grow without flowers
Different flowers on one plant can be at different stages
check.why: Each flower on a plant has its own little life. Some are buds, some have just opened, and some have already become fruits. Picking 'lemons grow without flowers' misses that each small lemon is where a flower was, a little earlier.

activities.title: Make a Life Cycle Wheel
activities.context: In this activity you make a paper wheel that turns. Through a window you see one stage of a plant's life at a time, and the stages go round and round.

materials.item: 2 paper plates, or 2 circles cut from a cereal box, the size of a steel plate
crayons or colour pencils
scissors
a split pin, or a 3 cm piece of drinking straw, or a needle and thread to join the middles

activities.safety: A grown-up makes the hole in the middle with a pencil point.

schedule.what: Draw the six stages, cut a window and join the wheel.

activities.record: Turn the wheel and tell the life cycle to someone, starting from any stage.

setup.art: A paper plate divided into six slices like a cake, each with a drawing: seed, seedling, plant, flower, fruit, seeds.
setup.caption: 1. Divide one plate into 6 slices and draw a stage in each.

setup.art: A second paper plate with one slice-shaped window cut out.
setup.caption: 2. Cut a window the size of one slice in the other plate.

setup.art: The two plates joined in the middle, a child turning the top plate so the window shows the flower stage.
setup.caption: 3. Join the middles. Turn the top plate to go round the cycle.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Life Cycle Wheel. You draw the six stages of a plant's life on a plate.
flow.do: 1. On one plate, draw lines through the middle to make 6 equal slices, like a cake. 2. Choose a plant, like moong, sunflower or mango. 3. In each slice, in order going round, draw: seed, seedling, grown plant, flower, fruit, new seeds.
flow.say: Draw each stage in its own slice, going round in order. Which slice comes after the new seeds?
flow.kid: Draw 6 slices on one plate. Pick a plant. Draw one stage in each slice, going round in order.

flow.do: 1. On the second plate, cut out a window the size of one slice. 2. A grown-up makes a hole in the middle of both plates with a pencil point. 3. Push a split pin through both. Or push a short piece of straw through, snip each end into four little flaps, and press them flat. Or tie a big knot of thread on each side.
flow.say: Now the top plate can turn, and the window will show one stage at a time.
flow.kid: Cut a window in the second plate, one slice big. Ask a grown-up to make a hole in the middles. Join the plates.

flow.do: Turn the wheel slowly, and ask your child to tell the plant's life, stage by stage.
flow.say: Start at the flower this time. Tell me what happens next, and next, until you are back at the flower.
flow.kid: Turn the wheel. Start at the flower. Tell the story until you get back to the flower.

check.q: You turn your wheel to 'new seeds'. What comes next as you keep turning?
options: Flower
Seed, and then seedling again
The end
check.why: The new seeds are the start of new plants. Each one can sprout into a seedling, so the wheel goes round again. Picking 'the end' usually means seeing a plant's life as a line. One plant dies, but the cycle carries on in their seeds.

activities.title: New Plants Without Seeds: onion, money plant and potato
activities.context: Not every new plant starts as a seed. In this 10-day activity you grow new plants from an onion, a money plant stem and a potato, and watch roots and shoots appear.

materials.item: a small onion, if you can, one with a green tip already showing
a money plant stem with at least 2 leaves, cut by a grown-up from a plant
an old potato with eyes
2 small glasses or jars, and an old bottle
3 toothpicks

activities.safety: A grown-up cuts the money plant stem. Do not eat the onion or potato after the test.

schedule.what: Set up the onion, the money plant stem and the potato.
Change the onion's water. Look for roots.
Change the water. Look for roots and shoots on all three. Draw.
Change the water. Look again. Draw.
Compare all three. Draw them. Plant the best one in soil.

activities.record: Draw all three on days 1, 5 and 10. Write when you first saw roots, and when you first saw green shoots.

setup.art: An onion sitting on the mouth of a glass of water, its flat bottom just touching the water.
setup.caption: 1. Sit an onion on a glass so only its bottom touches the water.

setup.art: A money plant stem in a bottle of water, its lowest bump on the stem under the water.
setup.caption: 2. Put a money plant stem in water, with a stem bump under water.

setup.art: An old potato on a windowsill with small shoots growing from its eyes.
setup.caption: 3. Leave a potato with eyes in a warm place. Watch the eyes sprout.

flow.context: This is the first step of New Plants Without Seeds. You set up an onion, a money plant stem and a potato to grow new plants.
flow.do: 1. Onion: fill a small glass to the top with water. Sit the onion on it, flat roots end down, so only the bottom touches the water. If the glass is wide, push 3 toothpicks into the onion to hold it up. 2. Money plant: take off the leaves near the bottom of the stem. Stand it in a bottle of water so one bump on the stem is under water. 3. Potato: put it on a windowsill or in a warm basket.
flow.say: None of these is a seed. Let's see if each one can still grow a new plant.
flow.kid: Sit the onion on a glass of water. Only its bottom touches. Put the money plant stem in water. Put the potato somewhere warm.
flow.parent: The bumps on a money plant stem are where roots grow from. Some shop onions are treated so they do not sprout. Choose one that already has a green tip, or try two onions. A garlic clove, pointed end up, also works.

flow.do: 1. Pour away the onion's water and give it fresh water, so it does not smell. 2. Look for white roots and green shoots on all three. 3. Draw them on day 5.
flow.say: Which one grew first? Where are its new roots coming from?
flow.kid: Change the onion's water. Look for white roots and green shoots. Which grew first? Draw them on day 5.
flow.parent: What to expect. Onion: white roots in 2 to 4 days and green shoots within a week. Money plant: small roots in 7 to 14 days, from the bump under water. Potato: shoots from its eyes in 1 to 3 weeks, faster in a warm dark place. Choose an old potato that already has small bumps at its eyes. If it has not sprouted by day 10, keep watching for another week. If the onion goes soft or smelly, it was sitting too deep. Start again with only its bottom in the water.

flow.do: 1. Compare all three. 2. Talk about how they are different from seeds. 3. Plant the onion or the money plant in a pot of soil if you like.
flow.say: These new plants grew from pieces of old plants. Will the new money plant look like their parent?
flow.kid: Compare all three. They grew from pieces, not seeds. Will the new plant look like their parent?

check.q: A new money plant grows from a stem cutting. How will the new plant compare with the plant the stem came from?
options: They will be an exact copy, a clone
They will be a different kind of plant
They will need seeds to grow
check.why: A cutting carries exactly the same instructions as their parent, so they grow into a copy. Picking 'a different kind' is a fair worry. But a seed can mix instructions from two parents, and a cutting does not.

flow.think: If every plant in a field is a copy of the same plant, what happens if a disease comes that they cannot fight?

activities.title: Eat the Life Cycle: which part of the plant is on your plate?
activities.context: In this activity you look at the food on your plate, or in your kitchen, and work out which part and which stage of a plant each food comes from.

materials.item: a meal, or about 12 foods from the kitchen
a sheet of paper with 6 columns: seeds, fruits, flowers, leaves, stems, roots

activities.safety: Only taste foods that a grown-up says are ready to eat.

schedule.what: Sort the foods by which part of the plant they come from.

activities.record: Fill the six columns. Try to find at least one food for every column.

setup.art: A banana leaf with rice, sambar, bhindi poriyal, a chapati, cucumber slices and a little salt, seen from above.
setup.caption: 1. Look at a meal, or collect 12 foods from the kitchen.

setup.art: A sheet with six columns, each with a picture: a seed, a fruit, a flower, a leaf, a stem and a root.
setup.caption: 2. Make a sheet with six columns: seeds, fruits, flowers, leaves, stems, roots.

setup.art: A child placing a cauliflower floret under the flower column and a potato under the stem column.
setup.caption: 3. Put each food in its column. Watch for the tricky ones.

flow.context: This is the first step of Eat the Life Cycle. You collect foods and get ready to sort them by plant part.
flow.do: 1. Collect about 12 foods. Try rice, dal, atta, a tomato, bhindi and a potato. Add an onion, palak, a carrot, a cauliflower, jeera and a banana. 2. Draw the six columns.
flow.say: Every food here came from a plant. But which part of the plant? And which stage of their life?
flow.kid: Collect 12 foods. Draw six columns: seeds, fruits, flowers, leaves, stems, roots. Where does each food go?

flow.do: Sort each food into its column together. Talk about the tricky ones.
flow.say: Is a potato a root? Have a look at its eyes. Roots don't have eyes like that. Stems do.
flow.kid: Put each food in its column. Some are tricky! Look closely before you choose.
flow.parent: Answers. Seeds: rice, wheat in atta, dal, jeera, rai, peanuts, coffee. Fruits: tomato, bhindi, brinjal, cucumber, chilli, mango, banana, drumstick. Flowers: cauliflower and broccoli are flower buds, and banana flower is cooked in many parts of India. Cloves are dried flower buds, and saffron threads come from the middle of a flower. Leaves: palak, methi, cabbage, curry leaves, tea, and the layers of an onion. Stems: potato, ginger, sugarcane. Roots: carrot, radish, beetroot, sweet potato.

check.q: Which part of the plant is a cauliflower?
options: A root
A fruit
A bunch of tiny flower buds
check.why: The white head of a cauliflower is hundreds of tiny flower buds packed tightly together. If you leave a cauliflower plant growing, the buds can open into small yellow flowers. Picking 'a fruit' is a fair guess, because we eat it like a vegetable. But it has no seeds inside, because the flowers have not opened yet.

flow.do: Count how many foods are in each column.
flow.say: Which column has the most foods? Which stage of a plant's life do we eat most?
flow.kid: Which column has the most? Which stage of a plant's life do we eat most?
flow.think: Rice, wheat and dal are all seeds, each packed with food for a young plant. Why do you think seeds make such good food for us too?

activities.title: Life Cycle Flipbook
activities.context: In this activity you draw a plant's life cycle on a stack of small pages, changing it a little on each page. When you flip the pages fast, the plant grows, flowers, makes fruit and drops their seeds.

materials.item: 16 small pieces of paper of the same size, such as a small notepad, or an A4 sheet cut into 16
a pencil
a stapler, a binder clip or a strong rubber band

activities.safety: A grown-up helps with the stapler.

schedule.what: Draw 16 pages, bind them and flip.

activities.record: Flip your book for someone, and tell them what is happening on each part.

setup.art: A stack of small papers, with a ground line drawn in the same place near the bottom of each one.
setup.caption: 1. Draw a ground line in the same place on all 16 pages.

setup.art: A row of small pages showing a seed, then a sprout, a taller plant, a bud, a flower, a fruit and falling seeds.
setup.caption: 2. Draw the plant a little bigger on each page, all the way round to seeds.

setup.art: A child's thumb flipping a small stapled flipbook, the pages blurring.
setup.caption: 3. Staple the pages at one end. Flip them fast.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Life Cycle Flipbook. You get 16 pages ready to draw on.
flow.do: 1. Make 16 small pages the same size. 2. On every page, draw a ground line in the same place, near the bottom. You can trace it through the page underneath.
flow.say: A flipbook works because each picture is only a little different from the last. Let's plan the 16 pages first.
flow.kid: Get 16 small pages. Draw a ground line on each one, in the same place. Trace it so it matches.

flow.do: Draw one stage per page. For example: pages 1 and 2, a seed. 3 and 4, a sprout. 5 to 7, a growing plant. 8, a bud. 9 and 10, an open flower. 11, petals falling. 12 and 13, a fruit growing. 14, a ripe fruit. 15, seeds falling. 16, a new sprout.
flow.say: Make each picture just a little bigger than the one before. Trace the last picture, then add a bit.
flow.kid: Draw the plant a little bigger on each page. Trace the one before, then add a bit. End with a new sprout!
flow.parent: Younger children can make 8 pages instead of 16. Tracing the previous page through the paper makes the flipbook smoother.

flow.do: 1. Put the pages in order, page 1 on top. 2. Staple or clip one end. 3. Flip the pages fast with your thumb.
flow.say: Watch it go! Now flip it again, but start thinking from the flower. Where does the story end?
flow.kid: Staple one end. Flip fast with your thumb! Your plant grows, flowers and makes seeds.
flow.think: Your flipbook ends with a new sprout. If you kept drawing, would it ever really end?

activities.title: Adopt a Tree for a Year
activities.context: Trees go round part of their life cycle every year: new leaves, flowers, fruits and seeds. In this activity you choose one tree near your home and visit them once a month, for a year.

materials.item: a tree near your home that you can visit, such as a mango, neem, gulmohar, amaltas, jamun or peepal
a notebook to be the tree's diary
a phone camera, if you have one

activities.safety: Visit with a grown-up. Do not climb the tree.

schedule.what: Choose your tree, name them, and make their first diary page. Then visit once a month.

activities.record: Every month, one diary page: the date, a drawing or photo, and ticks for new leaves, buds, flowers, unripe fruit, ripe fruit and falling seeds.

setup.art: A child standing under a gulmohar tree with a notebook, looking up at their branches.
setup.caption: 1. Choose one tree near home that you can visit every month.

setup.art: A diary page with a drawing of the tree and tick boxes for leaves, buds, flowers, fruit and seeds.
setup.caption: 2. Make a diary page: draw them and tick what you see.

setup.art: Four small drawings of the same mango tree: bare-ish in winter, covered in flowers in February, with green mangoes in April, and ripe mangoes in May.
setup.caption: 3. Visit every month. Watch them flower and fruit through the year.

flow.context: This is the first step of Adopt a Tree. You choose a tree near your home to watch for a whole year.
flow.do: 1. Walk to a few trees nearby and choose one. 2. Find out their name, by asking a neighbour or using a plant app. 3. Give them a nickname too.
flow.say: This tree will be our friend for a whole year. We'll visit them every month and see what stage of their year they are in.
flow.kid: Choose a tree near home. Find out their name. Give them a nickname. You will visit them every month for a year.

flow.do: 1. Draw or photograph the whole tree, and one close-up of a branch. 2. Tick what you see: new leaves, buds, flowers, unripe fruit, ripe fruit, falling seeds. 3. Write the date.
flow.say: What is the tree doing right now? Are they flowering, fruiting, or resting?
flow.kid: Draw your tree. Draw one branch up close. Tick what you see. Write the date.
flow.parent: Many Indian trees flower before or just after the hot season. Mango flowers around January to March and fruits in April to June. Neem flowers around March and April. Amaltas is covered in yellow flowers in April and May. Gulmohar turns red in April to June. A project called SeasonWatch collects records like these from children all over India.
flow.think: A moong plant goes round their life cycle once and dies. Your tree flowers and fruits again every year. Is the tree's year a life cycle too?

projects.title: Kitchen to Kitchen: grow moong from seed to seed
projects.context: In this project, which takes about two and a half months, you sow moong from your kitchen jar. You look after them as they grow, flower and make pods, and you harvest a handful of new moong. That is one whole life cycle.

materials.item: 8 whole green moong seeds from the kitchen, the kind you sprout
a pot or tub at least 20 cm deep and 20 cm wide, with holes in the bottom. An old paint bucket or a grow bag works
soil, mixed with a few handfuls of compost if you have it
a sunny spot that gets at least 5 hours of direct sun a day
a ruler, a notebook for the plant's diary, and some thread

projects.safety: A grown-up makes holes in the bottom of a bucket. Wash your hands after touching soil. Do not use pesticide sprays.

schedule.what: Soak 8 moong seeds overnight. Fill the pot. Name your plant.
Sow the seeds 2 cm deep. Water them. Put the pot in the sun.
Look for seed leaves and true leaves. Keep the 3 or 4 strongest plants. Measure.
Measure the tallest plant. Draw it.
Measure. Draw. Look for buds at the tips.
Flowers! Count them. Write the date of the first flower.
Pods! Tie a thread on the first pod. Measure it.
Measure. Are any pods turning brown or black?
Pick the black, dry pods. Dry them in the sun for 2 days.
Open the pods. Count the seeds. Make your graph.
Sow some new seeds to start again. Sprout and eat some. Read your diary aloud.

projects.record: A diary page every week: the date, a drawing, the height of the tallest plant, and the number of flowers or pods. At the end, a line graph of height, and the total number of seeds.

setup.art: A child pressing soaked moong seeds 2 cm deep into a soil-filled paint bucket on a sunny balcony, a name label 'Hari' on the bucket.
setup.caption: 1. Sow soaked moong 2 cm deep in a deep pot in full sun.

setup.art: The same bucket a month later, with bushy moong plants with leaves in threes and small yellow flowers at the top.
setup.caption: 2. Look after them. Flowers come after about a month.

setup.art: Black dry moong pods on the plant, and a child's hand opening one over a steel plate full of new green moong.
setup.caption: 3. Pick the black pods. Count your new moong seeds.

flow.context: This is the first step of Kitchen to Kitchen. You sow moong from the kitchen jar and give your plant a name.
flow.do: 1. Soak 8 moong seeds in water overnight. 2. Fill the pot with soil to 2 cm below the top. 3. Next day, push the seeds 2 cm deep, about 5 cm apart. 4. Water gently until water comes out of the bottom. 5. Put the pot in your sunniest spot. 6. Name the plant and draw page 1 of their diary.
flow.say: These seeds came from our kitchen. If we look after them, they will give us moong back. What shall we call our plant?
flow.kid: Soak 8 moong seeds overnight. Push them 2 cm into the soil. Water them. Put the pot in the sun. Give your plant a name!
flow.parent: Moong likes warm weather, about 25 to 35 degrees. In most of north India, sow them between February and August. In much of south India they grow most of the year. In north India's cold months, from November to January, grow matar instead. Matar flowers in about 6 to 8 weeks and makes dry seeds in about 3 months. The pot must get at least 5 hours of direct sun. In shade, moong grows tall and thin and may not flower at all. If you have no sunny spot, ask to use a relative's terrace or a school garden.

flow.do: 1. Look for the seedlings. 2. First come two fat seed leaves, then two plain leaves, and after that leaves in groups of three. 3. Around day 10, keep the 3 or 4 strongest plants. Snip the others at the soil with scissors, instead of pulling them.
flow.say: Look, their first leaves are fat and round. Those came from inside the seed. The new leaves have their own shape.
flow.kid: Find the seed leaves. They are fat and round. Then find the new leaves. Keep the 3 or 4 strongest plants.
flow.parent: Snipping is better than pulling, because pulling can tear the roots of the plants next to them. Water whenever the top 2 cm of soil feels dry to a finger. Never leave the pot standing in water.

flow.do: Once a week: 1. Measure the tallest plant from the soil to their top. 2. Draw them. 3. Write the number in the diary.
flow.say: How much did they grow this week? Are they growing faster or slower than last week?
flow.kid: Once a week, measure the tallest plant. Draw them. Write the number down. Did they grow fast or slow?
flow.parent: Tiny black or green insects on the tips are aphids. Wash them off with a gentle spray of water. Leaves with yellow patches may have a virus that is common in moong. Snip off that plant and keep the others. Heavy rain can rot the roots, so move the pot under a ledge in a storm.

flow.do: 1. Around day 30 to 40, look for small pale yellow flowers at the ends of short stalks. 2. Write the date of the first flower. 3. Count the flowers each week.
flow.say: Our plant is a grown plant now. They have stopped just making leaves. They are making flowers.
flow.kid: Look for small yellow flowers. Write the date of the first one. Count the flowers.
flow.parent: Moong flowers can pollinate themselves, so you do not need bees. The flowers are small and close by midday, so look in the morning.

flow.do: 1. A few days after flowering, look for thin green pods where the flowers were. 2. Tie a thread on the first pod. 3. Measure it each week.
flow.say: Where the flower was, there is now a pod. What do you think is growing inside it?
flow.kid: Find a thin green pod where a flower was. Tie a thread on it. Measure it. What is inside?

check.q: A thin green pod is growing where your moong flower was. What is the pod?
options: A root growing in the air
The fruit, which grew from the flower and holds the new seeds
A new leaf
check.why: The pod is the moong plant's fruit. It grew from the base of the flower, and the new moong seeds grow inside it. Picking 'a new leaf' is a fair guess, because the young pod is thin and green. But it hangs where the flower was, and if you open it there are tiny seeds in a row.

flow.do: 1. When pods turn black and dry, usually around day 55 to 75, pick them before they split. 2. Dry them in the sun on a plate for 2 days. 3. Open them over a plate. 4. Count the seeds in each pod and add them all up. 5. Draw a line graph of the plant's height, week by week.
flow.say: One seed went into the soil. How many have we got back? Let's count.
flow.kid: Pick the black pods before they pop open. Dry them in the sun. Open them. Count every seed!
flow.parent: Ripe moong pods can twist and pop open in the sun, flinging their seeds. Pick them as soon as they are black, or tie a small paper bag over a bunch. Each pod usually has about 10 to 15 seeds. The whole plant turns yellow and dries once their pods are ripe. That is the end of their life cycle, not a mistake.

check.q: Your moong plant turns yellow and dries up after their pods ripen. What has happened?
options: They have finished their life cycle, as all annual plants do
You did something wrong
They need more water
check.why: Moong is an annual. They go from seed to seed in one season, then die. Their new seeds carry the life cycle on. Picking 'you did something wrong' is a natural worry. But a yellow, dry moong plant with black pods has done exactly what they were meant to do.

flow.do: 1. Sow some of your new seeds in the pot again, to start the next circle. 2. Soak and sprout some to eat. 3. Put the old plants in a compost pit or bin. 4. Read the diary aloud to the family.
flow.say: We are back where we started, with moong seeds. Shall we start the next circle?
flow.kid: Sow some new seeds to start again. Sprout some to eat. Put the old plant in compost. Read your diary to your family.
flow.parent: If the plants die early, from too little sun, too much water or pests, that is sad. It is all right to feel sad. Write a short note to the plant, and talk about what they needed. Then try again in the right season.
flow.think: The old moong plant goes into the compost. Their atoms go back to the soil and air. Could some of them end up in the next moong plant?

challenges.title: Be the Bee: design a pollen mover
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. Flowers need pollen carried to their middle before they can make fruit. You design and test the best tool for carrying pollen, the way Edmond did with a splinter and his thumb.
challenges.problem: On a high balcony, few bees and butterflies visit. Your job is to design the best tool for picking up pollen from one flower and leaving it on another, without hurting the flowers.
constraints: It must not tear or bruise the petals.
It must be made from things you have at home.
Test every tool the same way: touch the pollen 3 times, then tap the tool 3 times on a sheet of dark paper.
materials: a flower with lots of loose yellow pollen, such as a hibiscus, a lily, a sunflower or a pumpkin flower
things to test: a cotton bud, a soft paintbrush, a feather, a fingertip, a woollen thread, a pipe cleaner or a bit of fluffy cloth
a magnifying glass, if you have one
general: A soft paintbrush or a cotton bud, which gardeners use.
Gently shaking a plant like tomato or chilli in the morning, so pollen falls inside each flower.
creative: A fuzzy pipe cleaner bent into a bee shape. Bees carry pollen on the fluffy hairs all over their bodies.
An electric toothbrush, switched on and held against a tomato flower's stalk. The shaking makes pollen fall, the way big bees buzz tomato flowers. Some tomato growers use vibrating tools like this.
In 2020, scientists in Japan blew soap bubbles with pollen in them onto pear flowers. Some of the flowers grew fruit.
challenges.your_turn: Now invent your own pollen mover. Draw it, make it, and test it the same way. Does it beat the others?

setup.art: A red hibiscus flower with its long middle column dusted with yellow pollen.
setup.caption: 1. Find a flower with lots of yellow pollen.

setup.art: A row of tools on a table: a cotton bud, a paintbrush, a feather, a pipe cleaner and a woollen thread.
setup.caption: 2. Collect tools to test.

setup.art: A cotton bud tapping a sheet of black paper, leaving yellow specks, next to fewer specks from a feather.
setup.caption: 3. Touch the pollen 3 times, tap on dark paper 3 times. Compare.

flow.context: This is the first step of Be the Bee. You look closely at the pollen on a flower.
flow.do: 1. Look at the flower with your child. 2. Find the pollen. 3. Touch it gently with a fingertip and look at the yellow dust that comes off.
flow.say: This yellow dust is pollen. A bee carries it from flower to flower without even trying. Let's see how hard it is for us.
flow.kid: Find the yellow dust in the flower. That is pollen. Touch it gently. Look at your fingertip.
flow.parent: Hibiscus pollen grains are big enough to see as separate specks with a magnifying glass. Lily pollen stains clothes orange, so take care.

flow.do: Before testing, help your child draw or write three ideas for a pollen mover.
flow.say: Think like an engineer. What would carry pollen best? Something fluffy, something smooth, or something sticky?
flow.kid: Think like an engineer! Draw three ideas for a pollen mover. Fluffy, smooth or sticky?

flow.do: 1. Test each tool the same way: touch the pollen 3 times, then tap it 3 times on the dark paper. 2. Write the tool's name beside its spot. 3. Compare the spots: lots, some or few yellow specks.
flow.say: Same test for every tool. Which one picks up and drops off the most pollen?
flow.kid: Test each tool. Touch the pollen 3 times. Tap the paper 3 times. Which leaves the most yellow specks?

check.q: Why are bees so good at carrying pollen?
options: They eat the pollen and spit it out
They are very big
Their bodies are covered in fluffy hairs that pollen sticks to
check.why: A bee's body is covered in branched hairs. Pollen sticks to them as she crawls through a flower, and brushes off on the next flower. Picking 'they eat it and spit it out' is a fair guess, because bees do eat pollen. But the pollen that reaches the next flower is mostly the dust stuck on their hairs.

flow.do: Read the usual ideas and the creative ideas together. Then invent a new one and test it.
flow.say: Here is what gardeners usually do, and some surprising ideas. Can you invent something better?
flow.kid: Read the usual ideas and the creative ones. Now invent your own pollen mover. Can it beat them?
flow.think: Bees, butterflies, birds and bats do this job for free, all over the world. What would it cost if people had to do it all by hand?

challenges.title: The Never-Empty Balcony: plan a garden that is always flowering
challenges.context: This is a planning challenge. You use what you know about how long different plants take to go round their life cycles, to plan pots that always have flowers or fruit.
challenges.problem: Plan 6 pots on a balcony or windowsill so that, from June to March, something is always flowering or fruiting. That is good for bees and butterflies, and it gives your family food.
constraints: At least 2 pots must grow food.
Use the table of how long each plant takes, and show your sowing dates on a calendar.
materials: the table of plants in this challenge
general: Mix quick plants, like moong and methi, with ones that live for years and keep flowering, like tulsi, chilli and hibiscus.
Sow a quick crop in small batches, two weeks apart. Then a new batch is always coming up. Farmers call this succession sowing.
Grow warm-weather plants, like bhindi and moong, in summer and the monsoon, and cool-weather plants, like matar and marigold, in winter.
creative: Save seeds from each crop and sow them for the next season, so your balcony goes round its own life cycle every year.
Grow plants that flower at different times of day: morning flowers like bhindi, and evening flowers like lauki and raat ki rani.
Add a small dish of water with stones in it, so bees have somewhere safe to drink.
challenges.your_turn: Now draw your own balcony plan. Mark the sowing date and the flowering months for each pot. Is there any month with no flowers? Fix it.

setup.art: A sheet with six pot outlines drawn on it, each waiting for a plant name.
setup.caption: 1. Draw your 6 pots.

setup.art: A calendar from June to March with coloured bars showing when each plant flowers.
setup.caption: 2. Use the table to mark when each plant will flower.

setup.art: A balcony with six pots: tulsi, chilli and marigold in flower, moong with pods, and a bee visiting.
setup.caption: 3. Check that every month has something flowering.

flow.context: This is the first step of The Never-Empty Balcony. You read a table of how long plants take to flower.
flow.do: Read the table together. It shows about how long each plant takes from sowing to their first flowers.
flow.say: Every plant has their own speed round the life cycle. If we know the speeds, we can plan.
flow.kid: Read the table. Which plant flowers fastest after sowing? Which is slowest?

chart.title: About how long from sowing to the first flowers (rough numbers, which change with the weather and the kind of seed)
rows: Most of the year, best in the cool months
Many weeks, if you pick old flowers
On and off for 2 years or more

flow.do: Help your child choose 6 plants. Mark on the calendar when each will be sown and when they will flower.
flow.say: Let's colour each plant's flowering months. Are there any empty months?
flow.kid: Choose 6 plants. Colour the months each one will flower. Look for empty months.

check.q: You sow methi in one big batch in October. They flower for a few weeks and then they are finished. How could you keep having methi flowers for longer?
options: Water them twice as much
Sow a small batch every two weeks
Sow all the seeds in one pot
check.why: Each batch goes round its life cycle on its own timetable. Sowing a little every two weeks means a new batch is always coming into flower. Picking 'water them twice as much' cannot change how long an annual's life cycle is. Too much water can even rot them.

flow.do: Read the usual and the creative ideas together. Then fix any empty months in the plan.
flow.say: Which month was hardest to fill? What could fill it?
flow.kid: Which month was empty? What could you grow to fill it? Fix your plan.
flow.think: Farmers plan by life cycles too. Why do you think many farmers sow rice at the start of the monsoon?

quiz.p: Which is the right order for a flowering plant's life cycle?
opts: Seed, seedling, grown plant, flower, fruit, new seeds
quiz.why: A seed sprouts into a seedling, grows into a grown plant, makes flowers, and each flower can become a fruit holding new seeds. Picking 'seed, flower, seedling' puts the flower too early. A plant must grow big before they can flower.

opts: A very young plant just out of their seed
quiz.why: A seedling has just sprouted, with a tiny root, a short stem and their first leaves. Picking 'a seed in a packet' mixes up the seed and the seedling. The seedling is the next stage.

quiz.p: A fruit grows from which part of a plant?
quiz.why: After pollen reaches the middle of a flower, the flower's base swells into the fruit. Picking 'the leaf' is a guess some children make because fruits hang among the leaves. But each fruit is where a flower was.

quiz.p: The green cap on a brinjal is…
opts: Left over from the brinjal's flower
quiz.why: It is made of the sepals, the small green leaves that wrapped the flower bud. They stay on as the fruit grows. Picking 'a leaf that grew later' is a fair guess, because it is green. But it was there first, around the flower.

quiz.p: To a scientist, which of these is a fruit?
quiz.why: Bhindi grows from a flower and has seeds inside, so it is a fruit. A potato is a swollen stem, a carrot is a root and palak is a leaf. Picking potato is common, because we eat both potatoes and bhindi as vegetables. But a potato has no seeds and did not grow from a flower.

quiz.p: Why is a plant's life called a CYCLE?
opts: Because the new seeds start the same stages again, going round
quiz.why: The new seeds are the start of new plants, so the stages go round in a circle. Picking 'it only happens once' is true for one plant. But their seeds carry the cycle on.

quiz.p: A moong plant's pods turn black, and the plant turns yellow and dries up. What happens next in the life cycle?
opts: The pods turn back into flowers
The seeds in the pods can grow into new moong plants
quiz.why: The old plant has finished, but their seeds start the next circle. Picking 'nothing, it is over' looks at the old plant only, and forgets their seeds.

quiz.p: You tag 5 flowers on a chilli plant. After a week, 3 have become baby chillies and 2 have fallen off. What should you write in your results?
opts: 3 out of 5 flowers became fruits, and 2 fell off
quiz.why: Every result counts, including the flowers that fell. Not every flower becomes a fruit, and that is worth knowing. Picking 'only the 3 that worked' would hide part of what really happened. Scientists write down everything they see.
quiz.context: In the Flower to Fruit experiment, you tie threads on open flowers and check them every day.

quiz.p: Look at the line graph of a bhindi pod. How long was it on day 6?
quiz.why: Find day 6 along the bottom, go up to the line, then across to the side. It reads 10 cm. Picking 6 cm means reading the day number as the length.
quiz.context: In the Flower to Fruit experiment, you measure a young bhindi pod every day, from its stalk to its tip.

chart.title: Made-up example: length of a tagged bhindi pod, day by day
chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a bhindi pod often does. Your plant will be different.

quiz.p: Which plant finishes their whole life cycle, from seed to new seeds, in 2 to 3 months?
quiz.why: Moong is an annual and goes from seed to seed in two to three months. Mango, neem and coconut are perennials that take years to first flower. Picking mango may come from thinking fruit trees are quick, because mangoes come every summer. But a mango tree takes years to start.

quiz.p: Which of these can grow a new plant WITHOUT a seed?
quiz.why: A potato is a swollen stem, and each eye can sprout a new plant, a copy of their parent. The others are all seeds. Picking a rice grain is a natural mistake, because we think of rice as food, not as seeds. But each rice grain is a seed, and they can sprout into a rice plant.

quiz.p: Where does most of a big tree's body come from?
opts: Carbon dioxide from the air, and water, put together using sunlight
quiz.why: Leaves build sugar from carbon dioxide and water, using sunlight, and the tree builds their wood from that sugar. Picking 'the soil' is what almost everyone guesses. But a famous test showed a willow gained about 75 kilograms while their soil lost only about 60 grams.

quiz.p: In the Floating Leaves experiment, leaf circles floated up in bright light but stayed down in the dark. What made them float?
opts: Bubbles of oxygen the leaf made using light
quiz.why: In light, leaves make sugar and give out oxygen, and the bubbles lift the circles. Both glasses had the same soap, so the soap cannot explain the difference. Only the light was different.
quiz.context: In the Floating Leaves experiment, you make small circles of palak leaf sink in water with a pinch of baking soda. One glass sits in bright light, one in the dark.

chart.title: Made-up example: leaf circles floating after 20 minutes (out of 10 in each glass)
chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what often happens. Your numbers will be different.

quiz.p: What happens to a plant's body after they die?
opts: Decomposers break them down, and their atoms go back to the soil and air for new life
quiz.why: Fungi, bacteria and small animals eat the dead plant. Its carbon goes back into the air and its minerals into the soil, where new plants use them. Picking 'it vanishes' usually means thinking matter can disappear. It cannot. It changes form.

quiz.p: Do scientists know how bamboo counts about 48 years before they flower?
opts: No, it is still a mystery
Yes, they have a clock in their roots
quiz.why: Nobody knows how bamboo keeps time for so long. There are ideas, but none has been proved. Picking 'they count the monsoons' is a clever guess that some people have made. But nobody has shown it is true.

quiz.p: Who found the way to make vanilla flowers grow pods outside Mexico, using a thin stick and his thumb?
quiz.why: Edmond Albius found the method in 1841, on the island now called Réunion. It is still used today. Picking Darwin is a common guess, because he studied plants and flowers. But he did not find this.
quiz.context: Vanilla pods are the fruits of an orchid flower. Outside Mexico, the flowers used to drop off without making pods.

applications: Farmers plan sowing and harvest by each crop's life cycle: rice in the monsoon, wheat and mustard in winter.
Farmers save seeds from one harvest to sow the next year, so their crops go round the cycle again.
Seed companies print 'days to harvest' on seed packets, so gardeners know how long each life cycle takes.
Vanilla farmers in Madagascar, Réunion, Kerala and Karnataka pollinate every flower by hand, using Edmond Albius's method.
Pumpkin, cucumber and gourd growers on terraces move pollen by hand when bees are few.
Fruit farmers grow mango, guava and lemon trees from grafts and cuttings, so the fruit is exactly like the parent's.
Potatoes, sugarcane, bananas and roses are grown from pieces of the plant instead of seeds.
Flower growers use lights at night to stop or start flowering, because many plants measure the length of the night.
Plant breeders cross plants by moving pollen by hand, to make new kinds of rice, wheat and vegetables.
Compost pits turn dead plants and kitchen peels back into rich soil for the next crop.
Seed banks keep seeds of thousands of kinds of plant, so their life cycles can be started again if a crop is lost.
Citizen-science projects like SeasonWatch ask children to record when trees flower and fruit, to track how the climate is changing.
Space agencies grow plants from seed to seed on space stations, to plan farms on the Moon and Mars.

open_questions.q: How does bamboo count about 48 years before they flower, and how do clumps far apart stay in step?
open_questions.why_open: Nobody has found a clock that could count so long inside a plant. There are ideas, but none has been proved.

open_questions.q: Why did flowering plants spread so fast and take over the land?
open_questions.why_open: Darwin called it 'an abominable mystery' in 1879. Scientists still argue about how much was due to insects, fast growth, fruits or the climate.

open_questions.q: Exactly how does a plant decide that they are big enough to flower?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists know many of the signals: day length, cold, age and sugar. How the plant puts them all together is still being worked out.

open_questions.q: How long can a single plant live?
open_questions.why_open: Some trees are thousands of years old. Some plants, like grasses and aspen trees, spread as copies of themselves for so long that nobody knows where one plant ends.

open_questions.q: What is the best way to grow plants through their whole life cycle on the Moon or Mars?
open_questions.why_open: Plants have gone from seed to seed in space stations. But Moon and Mars soil is very different, and nobody has grown a crop there yet.

open_questions.q: How will a warmer world change when plants flower?
open_questions.why_open: Many plants now flower earlier than they used to. If they flower before their insects wake up, the flowers may make less fruit. How much this will happen, and where, is still being studied.

open_questions.q: Is a seed the same plant as their parent, or a new one?
open_questions.why_open: Biologists count them as a new plant, because they have a new mix of instructions. Some thinkers say the seed is the same life carrying on. It depends what you mean by 'the same'.

maths.problem: In the Kitchen to Kitchen project, a moong plant made 20 pods. Each pod had about 10 seeds. About how many seeds did one plant give back?
maths.explain: There are 20 pods, and each holds about 10 seeds. That is 20 groups of 10. 20 × 10 = 200. So one seed planted gave back about 200 seeds.
maths.context: In the Kitchen to Kitchen project, you grow moong from one seed all the way to new seeds, and count them.
maths.why_maths: Counting every seed one by one takes a long time. Multiplying the number of pods by the seeds in each pod tells you quickly how many seeds one plant gives back.

maths.problem: You sowed moong on 1 July. The first flower opened on 5 August. How many days did the plant take to flower?
maths.explain: July has 31 days. From 1 July to 31 July is 30 days. Then 1 August to 5 August is 5 more days. 30 + 5 = 35 days. That is 5 weeks.
maths.context: In the Kitchen to Kitchen project, you write the date you sow the moong and the date the first flower opens.
maths.why_maths: Knowing how many days each stage takes tells you how long a plant's life cycle is, and helps you plan when to sow.

maths.problem: Look at the chart of peas counted in five pea pods. How many peas were there altogether? Which pod had the most?
maths.answer: 32 peas altogether. Pod 4 had the most, with 8.
maths.context: In the Inside the Fruit experiment, you open pea pods and count the peas inside. Peas are the seeds of the pea plant.

maths.problem: Look at the line graph of a bhindi pod. It was 2 cm long on day 2 and 10 cm long on day 6. How much did it grow in those 4 days? About how much is that each day?
maths.answer: 8 cm in 4 days. That is about 2 cm each day.
maths.explain: 10 take away 2 is 8. So it grew 8 cm. It took 4 days, from day 2 to day 6. 8 shared between 4 days is 2. So it grew about 2 cm each day.

maths.why_maths: Measuring in centimetres, and finding the difference, turns 'it got bigger' into exactly how fast the fruit grew.

maths.problem: Neelakurinji flowered near Munnar in 2018. They flower every 12 years. Write the next three years they should flower.
maths.context: Neelakurinji is a shrub that grows in the hills of Kerala and Tamil Nadu. Their flowers turn whole hillsides blue, but only once every 12 years.
maths.why_maths: A plant that flowers on a regular beat makes a number pattern. Spotting the pattern lets you predict when the hills will turn blue again.

maths.problem: Look at the chart from the Floating Leaves experiment. In the light, 9 out of 10 leaf circles were floating after 20 minutes. What fraction is that? How many were still at the bottom?
maths.answer: 9 out of 10, which is nine tenths. 1 circle was still at the bottom.
maths.explain: There were 10 circles in the glass. 9 were floating. So the fraction floating is 9 out of 10, written 9/10, or nine tenths. 10 take away 9 is 1, so 1 was still at the bottom.
maths.context: In the Floating Leaves experiment, you sink 10 small circles of palak leaf in each of two glasses. One glass is in bright light and one is in the dark.

roots.context: We have been learning how a plant goes round from seed to flower to fruit and back to seed. Now we ask what that circle tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: Your tomato held perhaps 100 seeds, and one tomato plant grows dozens of tomatoes. Very few of those seeds will ever become plants. We eat most of them with the tomato, and birds, ants and mice eat seeds everywhere. So a plant makes far more seeds than they need, and the extra feeds other living things.
deep_truth.habit: We think of a seed as the start of a new plant, so a seed that never grows seems wasted. But most seeds become food instead, for birds, ants, mice and people. Rice, wheat and dal are seeds too.
deep_truth.evidence: In Inside the Fruit, one tomato held about 100 seeds and one bhindi about 60. One moong seed gives back about 200 seeds, yet a pot has room for only 3 or 4 plants. The Eat the Life Cycle sort shows how many of our foods are seeds.

three.who_am_i: Much of your body was built from seeds you ate: rice, wheat, dal and nuts. Each one is food a plant packed for their young.
three.what_is_life: A plant makes far more seeds than they need to carry on. The extra seeds feed many other lives.
three.what_is_this_world: The air you breathe out can become part of a leaf. Plants, people and soil are built from the same atoms, passed round and round.

roots.thread: A moong plant grows from one seed and gives back about 200. Only a few need to grow to keep moong going. The rest feed ants, birds and people, and the dead plant feeds the decomposers in the soil. Each plant's life cycle is joined to the lives of many others, by the food that passes between them. So one moong plant's life cycle feeds many other lives.

teachings.teaching: The boy Nachiketa says to his father: look at those who came before us, and those who are here now. Like grain, a person ripens and falls. Like grain, a person is born again.
teachings.link: Long ago, teachers in India looked at grain in the field and saw a circle: ripening, falling and sprouting again. You can watch the same circle in a pot of moong.

teachings.source: Gospel of Matthew 13:3-8, the parable of the sower
teachings.teaching: A farmer scatters seed. Some falls on the path, and birds eat it. Some falls on rocks or among thorns, and dies. Some falls on good soil, and gives back a hundred times as much.
teachings.link: The farmer knew what you found by counting: a plant makes many seeds, and only some grow. The seeds on the path never grew, but they fed the birds.

teachings.teaching: For everything there is a season. There is a time to be born and a time to die, a time to plant and a time to pull up what is planted.
teachings.link: Plants keep to their seasons. Many flower only when the nights are the right length, and annuals die once their seeds are ready.

science.text: A plant builds their body mostly from carbon dioxide in the air and water, using the energy of sunlight. Very little of it comes from the soil.
When living things die, decomposers break them down, and their atoms go back into the air and soil to be used by new life. The same atoms go round for billions of years.

other_view.view: A plant does not make extra seeds to feed others. Most seeds die or are eaten, so plants that made more seeds left more young. Over a very long time, that is why plants make so many. On this view, the seeds a bird eats are simply lost to the plant.

how_we_found_out.story: For a long time, most scholars in Europe did not believe that a flower needs pollen to make seeds. Farmers in ancient Iraq already knew that a date palm gives good dates only if pollen from a male tree reaches their flowers. But scholars did not think this was true of all plants. In Tübingen, in Germany, a doctor and botanist named Rudolf Jakob Camerarius tested it. He grew plants such as mulberry, maize and a small weed called annual mercury. He kept pollen away from the flowers that make seeds. A female mulberry tree with no male tree nearby made fruit, but their seeds were empty. Plants that got no pollen made no good seeds. Plants that got pollen did. In 1694 he wrote that pollen must reach a flower before it can make seeds. Other botanists argued against him for more than 30 years. Later tests, like a palm pollinated by hand in Berlin in 1749, showed he was right.
how_we_found_out.when: 1694 (his letter on the sex of plants, published in Tübingen)
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That plants make seeds without pollen, and have nothing like male and female parts. Camerarius kept pollen away from mulberry, maize and annual mercury, and they made no good seeds.
